That Mr. Speaker do now leave the chair for the House to go into committee of Ways and Means.
He said: A Dominion budget necessarily deals with two years-the year that is past and for which the Public Accounts have been submitted to parliament, and the year that is either currfent or, as in this case, just closed.
Public Accounts 1924-25
The Public Accounts for the financial year 1924-25 were tabled on the 11th of January last. In the budget speech delivered on the 24th of March, 1925, in making the estimate for the outcome of the year 1924-25, I followed the usual safe practice of estimating revenues yet to come as somewhat less than they would likely be and expenditures as somewhat greater.
The actual outcome of that year, as shown by the Public Accounts recently tabled, gives in round figures $2,800,000 more of ordinary revenue than was estimated. Ordinary expenditures were $808,000 less than were estimated; capital expenditures $1,500,000 less; special expenditures $209,000 less; and loans to the Canadian National Railways $8,00^000

The Budget-Mr. Robb
leas. The budget estimated an increase of debt for that year of some $13,000,000. In connection with this estimated increase of debt I now desire to offer a pleasing explanation. When the estimate for budget purposes was determined, an item of $7,500,000 for the Canadian National Railways in the supplementary estimates submitted to the House for that year was included as an expenditure. Three months later, when under consideration in the House, this item was, on the motion of a member of the government, struck out thus reducing by that amount the estimated increase of debt. The improvement in our revenues and the curtailment of expenditures in these and other minor services were sufficient to change an estimated increase of some $13,000,000 in the debt into a decrease of $345,589.29, as shown by the Public Accounts for that year.
Increase of $29,965,520 in Revenue
Coming now to the fiscal year 1925-26, four years of prudent administration, good crops and greater production at home, improved conditions and increased purchasing power abroad, enabled me to-day to present a financial statement as encouraging to Canadians as it must be gratifying to all interested in the progress and development of Canada. Throughout the year imports of raw material for Canadian industries have been well maintained, in a number of instances in excess of previous years; while from month to month during the year export trade increased, resulting in a steady growth of our favourable balance, which at the end of the fiscal year
exceeds $402,000,000. Nowhere are the results of this growing trade more accurately reflected than in the increased earnings of Canadian railways and in the annual statements of Canadian financial institutions and Canadian industrial corporations.
The actual ordinary revenues received up to and including March 31 last amounted to S367,958,495. The estimated revenue yet to come when the accounts for the year are finally closed is $8,841,505. This gives a total revenue of $376,800,000, an increase of some $29,965,520 over similar revenues for 1924-25.
Revenues and Expenditures
The revenue estimated from customs duties is $127,360,000, an increase of $19,200,000 over the previous year; from excise duties we expect $42,920,000, an increase of $4,300,000; we estimate that the revenue from excise taxes will be $95,500,000, an increase of $9,689,000; from income taxes we estimate $55,530,000, a decrease of $700,00 under the previous year; of arrears overdue under the former Business Profits War Tax Act we have collected some $1,150,000; from interests on investments we estimate a revenue of $8,270,000, a decrease of about $3,062,000; we expect to receive $30,334,000 as post office receipts, an increase of $1,540,000; and from all other sources we estimate a total of $15,736,000, being an increase of $541,000.
With the permission of the House, I shall place on Hansard a comparative summary of the two years' revenues by services; also a further statement showing the percentages of revenues to the total revenues for the year 1925-26.

Obviously, had we not the heavy railway and merchant marine expenditures and those expenditures which grew out of war conditions, our surpluses and other available resources might have been used in the reduction of war debt and would have permitted the showing of a lower figure for interest attributable to the war. On the other hand, during the war and demobilization periods large outlays were charged to ordinary expenses which, while not actual war cost, were directly attributable to war conditions. Even now there are heavy annual charges not taken into consideration in the summary submitted for which the war is responsible, for instance, the amount of $4,000,000 expended in the collection of war taxes has not been included, nor have the annual charges relating to the management of loans issued for war purposes and the expenses of refinancing maturing war loans. These latter charges and expenses may be estimated conservatively at $4,000,000. There might also be included the cost of housing the staffs connected with these services, which is now carried by the Public Works department.
The Budget-Mr. Robb

The Budget-Mr. Robb
The advance of $10,000,000 has been charged to the net debt of. the Dominion as a nonactive asset, in the same way as all railway cash loans have been treated. This advance covers the loss of $7,400,000 referred to and leaves $2,600,000 for capital purposes. It will therefore be seen that the public accounts for the year will include not only all government expenditures but also the total loss of the railways and an amount of $2,600,000 available for railway capital purposes, over and above which no further financial assistance was given.
Our total payments in respect of these railway corporations now reach $601,000,000, actual cash outlay charged to our national debt. This is exclusive of accumulated interest charges, as well as the capital cost of the original Canadian Government Railways. A large part of this sum represents provision for losses incurred, adding no value to the road. A very substantial amount, however, has been devoted to improvements in the road and equipment, which have materially enhanced the value of the lines. The improvement of $43,000,000 in earnings within a period of four years speaks for itself.
One estimate of the value of the government's investment in the Canadian National Railways, exclusive of Canadian Government Railways, is $375,000,000. This figure is arrived at after eliminating deficits and such overvaluations and inflations as were established on the occasion of the royal commission investigation of 1947 and the subsequent arbitration proceedings.
Whatever may ultimately be decided as a proper valuation for the government's investment in the system, the fact remains that a very substantial contribution has been made and included as a non-active asset in arriving at the net debt as shown in our public accounts. With the company to-day almost within striking distance of meeting its fixed charges due the public, the time should not be far distant when additions to our national debt for Canadian National Railway purposes will cease. Certainly we have in the railway situation, as affecting our Dominion finances, a much improved showing and a brighter outlook.
Fiscal Year 1926-27
To forecast revenues for the current year accurately is always difficult. Indications, however, point towards a year of increased revenues. The main estimates already submitted to parliament and the probable amount of the further supplementary estimates would give a fairly close indication of the expenditures for the year.

The main estimates for all services other than railways amount to $345,771,351. Advances to railways amount to $31,000,000, and advances to merchant marine $600,000, or a total of $31,600,000. To this must be added something for supplementary estimates. For this purpose I shall allow $4,500,000, being approximately the amount of last year's supplementary estimates, less sundry items amounting to some $4,500,000 which will not this year be required. I confidently hope, however, that, the amount will not be so large, and I warn my friends on both sides that I will do my best to keep it lower.
May I direct the attention of the House and of the country to the remarkable development which has taken place in Canada's trade. We closed the fiscal year with a favourable balance of over $402,000,000, w'hich constitutes a record for any year since the war period. Unrevised figures for the fiscal year ended March 31, last show our total trade to be $2,258,534,453, an increase of $380,000,000 over that of the fiscal year which ended March 31, 1925, when our total trade amounted to $1,878,000,000. Our exports have continued to exceed our imports, and for the year under review these exports totalled $1,330,000,000, as against $1,081,000,000, the year previous. This is an increase in our export trade of $249,000,000. Our imports during the fiscal year totalled $927,000,000, as compared with $796,000,000 for the previous year, or an increase of $130,000,000. Summarizing these figures, it is seen that the favourable balance of our exports over imports has this year increased from $284,000,000 to $402,695,000.
When comparing our trade from year to year, there are two points of particular interest. One is the general favourable balance; the other, the source of our expansion of trade. Statistical reports for the whole fiscal year have not reached such a stage of completion that the trade can be classified by countries. But the figures for the eleven months ending February 28 are available, and a comparison can be made between that period and the same period ending February 28,	1925.
During the eleven months of the last fiscal year the balance of exports over imports increased by $115,000,000. Of this increase, no less than $104,000,000, or 90 per cent of the favourable balance, is accounted for by empire trade. This, Sir, is ample vindication of the trade policy adopted by the government, and shows that our efforts should be increasingly directed towards the cultivation of trade within the empire and with countries favourably disposed towards commercial intercourse with Canada.

The Income Tax

Happily our financial and1 commerical position now enables us to make very substantial reductions in the income taxes. With a desire to make available new money for development, our proposals provide reductions all along the line. In the revision of the Income War Tax Act, a distinction has been made between yearly earnings and income derived from investments. The act is now presented in a new and less complicated form, one which will make the tax easier to calculate and, we believe, easier to pay.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would not like to go beyond this present year, but if it will sweeten the taste to hon. gentlemen, I may say that we hope, if the enactment meets with the approval of parliament that it may apply to the taxes which are now being collected, but that will depend on hon. gentlemen opposite as much as upon ourselves.
Proposed Changes in Customs Tariff and Taxation
Coming now to the resolutions which I shall submit to the House proposing customs tariff changes and reductions of taxation under the Special War Revenue Act and the Income War Tax Act, apart from certain modifications to meet the requirements of the West Indies and other trade agreements, the tariff changes proposed are not numerous. Prior to the appointment of the Tariff Advisory Board, certain tariff changes to meet new and growing conditions had been determined on, and these are embodied in the resolutions I shall place before you.
On cocoa beans it is proposed to increase the general tariff from $1.50 to $2.00 per hundred pounds, and a corresponding increase is made on certain cocoa products.
It is also proposed to make green coffee free under the British preferential tariff.
The rates on ginger, spices, nutmegs, mace and arrowroot are reduced in compliance with the terms of the West Indies agreement.
Bananas remain free under all tariffs but the Governor in Council is given power to impose a duty of 50 cents a bunch under the general and intermediate tariffs, leaving them free under the British preferential tariff when imported by ship direct,
It is proposed to reduce the rate on pineapples in air-tight tins from 1| cents a pound 
to one-half cent under the British preferential tariff.
The general tariff on fresh meats is to be increased one-half cent a pound.
To encourage the conservation of our timber resources, it is proposed to admit tree seeds for reafforestation free of duty.
The duty on sugar for refining purposes testing 96 degrees of polarization is reduced under the British preferential tariff 16.288 cents per hundred pounds, that is from 45 cents to 28.712 cents. Proportionate reductions are made in the duty on sugar of other degrees of polarization.
Angostura bitters, imported by ship direct, are to be admitted under the British preferential tariff at $5.00 a gallon as compared with the present duty of $10.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF HON. J. A. ROBB, MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my first word upon this occasion must be to express the regret which I feel and which I have no doubt is felt in every quarter of the House that the hon. member for West York (Sir Henry Drayton), who usually acts as financial critic on occasions such as the present, is absent from the House at this time through indisposition. It is a great loss to the House that the hon. member for West York is not present upon this occasion. He has a familiarity with national finance which few of us possess. He has a great grasp of all things pertaining to the Department of Finance and he is intimate with the various details of that department to an extent that few of us can boast. Therefore, I feel under some disadvantage at the present moment, and I sincerely ask the indulgence of the House as I proceed if in the remarks which I propose to deliver this afternoon I am guilty of sins either of commission or omission. But I will do my best to offer such criticism as appears to me to be proper in regard to the budget statement which has just been delivered to the House by the Minister of Finance of Canada (Mr. Robb).

There is apparently much jubilation on the government side this afternoon upon the presentation of the annual budget. Let me say that we on this side of the House are prepared to tender our congratulations upon any real achievement of the minister or of the government in respect to the financial condition which has prevailed and which still prevails in the Dominion of Canada. The jubilation is not felt exclusively upon the other side of the House; but if we refrain from giving this government credit for the satisfactory statement which in some respects has been presented to the House to-day, if we are inclined to think that the credit is due in the first instance to a munificent Providence and in the second instance to the virility, strength and efforts of the Canadian people, I think we shall not be far amiss having in mind the modest remarks with which the Minister of Finance concluded his address.
We realize quite as fully as does the government that this country has within the past season been blessed by Providence much more abundantly than in former years; yes, most marvellously blessed have we been in the abundance of crop which this country has yielded. I believe I am within the mark when I say that Providence has blessed Canada during the past season with a wheat yield in the western provinces unsurpassed both in quality and quantity, a yield which is to-day commanding a good price in the markets of the world and this fact constitutes the most important feature of our commercial success. I do not believe I am far wrong in making that statement. But fortunately it is not only in the prairie provinces of the west that Providence has blessed us. Ontario, this great central province of Canada, has also been blessed with a wonderful harvest. So far as Providence has seen fit to act in the matter, He has poured out on this country an abundance which we have not enjoyed for many years past and we are to-day reaping the benefits.
I believe the situation which I have tried to portray to the House has been reflected in every walk, in every avenue, in every branch of the industrial life of the people of the Dominion of Canada, and as a result we have had some return to a moderate prosperity which has not existed in this country during the past four years. I do not suggest for a moment that the return has been complete; I do not suggest for a moment that the return has been general throughout the Dominion; but I say this-and this is all I will say-that conditions are better in Canada to-day than they have been during the past

The Budget-Mr. Guthrie
four years. We on this side of the House congratulate the people of Canada on the improved condition which has recently arisen as compared with the unfortunate state of affairs that has prevailed during the past four years. Now, if we are not inclined to bestow much of the credit for this improvement on the government of the day, no one can complain. This country has improved to some extent, not on account of any effort of the government but in spite of the government. For if the prosperity of a country was ever hindered or delayed by an organization of human beings this country has been so hindered and delayed through the administration of the King government.
The Minister of Finance comes to this chamber to-day and presents a budget which I think we may say is from the financial point of view, reasonably satisfactory. The figures which he has just given to the House are figures on which I think we may fairly congratulate him. The outstanding points in his budget presentation are certainly two: he announces, in the first place, a reduction in income tax, and in the second place a reduction in the duty on motor trucks and automobiles.

The expenditure proposed by the government for the present fiscal year is also greater than the expenditure of last year. So that the government year by year is progressing on an ascending scale in the matter of national expenditures. If there is one thing which the people of this country demand at the present time, I think it is that the expenditure of the national government be cut down'. I know of no cry throughout the province; of Ontario more persistent than that government economy be exercised to the very last degree. We hear that cry in our provincial legislature, and we are pleased to note that the government of Ontario has put the finances of the province on such a footing that within a reasonable time that province will regain* its former financial stability. We hear the same cry in our municipalities, where there is a call for
greater economy. On the other hand, in the public services of Canada, there has been year by year under this government an annual increase in our expenditure.' I make that statement without fear of contradiction. Anyone who will take the trouble to examine the estimates laid on the table of the House for the present session will find, upon page after page of those estimates, thousands, tens of thousands, hundreds of thousands of dollars of proposed expenditures which might well be stricken out, without any great inconvenience or any injury to the public service.
I do not say that all the expenditures proposed in the estimates are unjustifiable; certainly not. I do say, however, that there are millions of dollars of suggested expenditures which might very well be deferred for some years to come without any inconvenience and with no ill effects on the Dominion.
The minister has at last begun to reduce the taxation from which the people of Canada suffer. It is a hard task and I commend him for what he has done. Although I have not all the figures before me he proposes, I believe, something substantial in the way of income tax reduction. But I may remind the Minister of Finance that he is a member of a government which owes the people substantial reduction in taxation. He is a member of a government which has greatly increased the direct taxation in the four years that have passed, and the time is certainly at hand now when a substantial reduction should take place. Let me point out to the minister that when the Meighen government went out of power we had a sales tax of one and one-half per cent on the manufacturer and one and one-half per cent on the jobber, which tax during the first year of the King administration was increased to four and a half per cent. During the next year it was increased to six per cent. Then when it was found that the tax had become so high that it actually impeded trade in Canada it was reluctantly reduced to five per cent. That was one increase in taxation on the people of the country which materially added to their burdens; and the King administration was responsible for that increase. I would point out to the government, further, that when they took office there was in force a two cent cheque tax which the King administration promptly increased to one dollar in respect of large cheques, thus raising an enormous additional revenue and greatly increasing the burdens of the country. This was the second increase. I point out, again, that when the King administration took charge of the affairs of the country we had no such thing as a tax on receipts; that was a
The Budget-Mr. Guthrie

device of hon. gentlemen opposite. It was the third increase. And now the time has come when the Minister of Finance announces, as though he had achieved a triumph, that he is going to take off the tax on receipts. That tax should never have been imposed in the first instance; it placed upon the people of Canada an unnecessary burden which, together with the other taxes I have mentioned, has increased from year to year as I can show from the figures of the government.
When we consider that the country has had the advantage of a favourable crop with high prices for farm produce prevailing, and when we reflect that general business has improved throughout Canada and that the government is in no immediate need of money, should special praise be bestowed upon a government for endeavouring to do now what it should have done one, two or three years ago? I said that the government had materially increased the burden of taxation in this country, and I make that statement on the strength of the government's own report. At page 47 of this year's Public Accounts there is a statement showing what the taxes have been. In the last year of the Meighen government, the amount collected in sales tax, cheque tax, transportation tax, and so forth-all the taxes that were in force then-was $73,000,000 odd. During the first year of the King administration those collections, increased to $106,000,000 odd. During the next year that amount had again risen to $120,000,000 odd. Last year there was a falling off because business was not being done in the country and they could not raise the revenue-there was a falling off in these taxes down to $85,000,000 odd. At the dose of the present fiscal year, March 31, last, as announced to-day by the Minister of Finance, these taxes amounted to some $95,000,000, an increase of $25,000,000 over the highest amount ever received by the Meighen administration under this branch of taxation.
Now, at the last general election the people made a demand1 for reduction of taxes and the government has at last heard that demand, and recognizing its justice has granted a partial measure of relief. So far as the income tax reduction is concerned, we welcome it; and the people will rejoice in it. But it is very late in coming. It should have come one, two or three years ago. And it could have come one, two or three years ago if the government had properly administered the affairs of the country, if it had pursued from the time it took office 'proper rules of economy, if it had cut down various expenditures,-I say, Sir, that if the government had properly administered the various
l Mr. Guthrie.]
departments of state midlions and millions, yes, perhaps hundreds of millions of dollars of taxation could have been taken off one, two or three years ago. If the administration of the Customs department had been what it should have been there would have been an increase of revenue from customs and excise duties sufficient to have allowed large reductions in taxation. I well recall, Mr. Speaker, the statement made in this House about a year ago by the Prime Minister when he induced us to grant him a large sum of money, $350,000 I think it was,-for what purpose? Because, he said, serious smuggling and other frauds on the customs were going on throughout the length and breadth of Canada and millions and millions of dollars were being lost to the treasury. Lost through what? Through lax administration, through carelessness in administering the affairs of that department, millions and millions of dollars annually were lost to the treasury, lost to the people. Had the administration of that department been what the country was entitled to expect, this much delayed announcement of tax reduction might have been made, one, two or three years ago, and the income tax cut for the benefit of the taxpayers instead of money being diverted into the pockets of smugglers both in this country and in the United States.
There are matters, Mr. Speaker, in the budget speech upon which, as I said before, I think the Minister of Finance may well be congratulated. The reduction in postage should naturally take place. This announcement has likewise been long delayed. The Post Office Department has shown a favourable balance for some time past. During the war it was necessary to increase the rate from two cents to three cents for the purpose of the treasury. But the war has been over for many years now. Postage is something which appeals to every member in the community, it directly affects every citizen, and I regret that the action of the government in reducing the postage rate has been somewhat tardy. Year after year the post office has produced an abundant revenue, year after year it has shown a handsome surplus. Now, Sir, I am one of those who believe that the post office is established for the convenience of the people, not as a money-making agency of government, and as soon as the post office can be maintained upon the basis of actual cost then the postage rates should be brought down to an absolute minimum. For the last four years, as I say, a handsome surplus has been obtained from the Post Office Department. Any time within that period

The Budget-Mr. Guthrie
this reduction might have taken place. Today we have a welcome, though a very tardy, announcement that the rate of postage is to be reduced from three cents to two cents.
But, Mr. Speaker, I fancy that when the people of the Dominion to-morrow read in the newspapers the budget statement of the Minister of Finance, the portions which will most attract attention, particularly the people in the provinces of Ontario and Quebec and eastern Canada generally, will be those in which the minister deliberately interferes with our fiscal policy. We in the province of Ontario represent more than one-third of the population of the Dominion, and we contribute to the treasury more than one-half of its receipts. Last year in customs duties alone out of a total revenue of $108,000,000 Ontario contributed no less than $56,000,000. Therefore Ontario has a vital interest in the affairs of this country as transacted in this parliament. But we are in the strange and unsatisfactory position to-day that we have in this chamber representing this great province of Ontario but one single member of the cabinet, and he a new-comer. We are under a serious disadvantage in this respect in the province of Ontario. The great province of Saskatchewan is represented upon the floor of this House by three ministers, all more or less pledged in one direction in regard to fiscal matters; all heading for the free trade goal, and we have at the same time to represent the province of Ontario but a single minister. He may be very able, he may be very capable, but I think the House will agree with me that the importunity of the present government proved the opportunity of the Minister of Labour (Mr. Elliott). I think he can sit in his chair and smile and say, "It is an ill wind that blows nobody good." I think also in relation to him we can all realize the truth of another old adage:	Some men
are born to greatness, some men achieve greatness, and some men have greatness thrust upon them.
Now, Sir, I have nothing but the highest opinion and regard for my hon. friend the Minister of Labour. I have known him for many years as a very able, and a very active lawyer, a credit to his profession. I have known him chiefly as a corporation lawyer in the city of London; but I should never have dreamt of him as a man to represent labour; I should never have dreamt of him as a man so.soon to become Acting Minister of Health; I should never have selected him as a man to become Acting Minister of the Department of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment as I noticed announced in the papers this morning. Well, honours are falling thick and fast upon
him. I wonder if he can successfully overtake the manifold duties of the various offices he is now called upon to discharge. Who knows but what he will soon be designated as Acting Minister of Trade and Commerce, then as Acting Postmaster General, or Secretary of State? But the fact I wish to emphasize is this, that the great province of Ontario is not fairly or adequately represented in this parliament to-day.

speechtext:
At all events we know quite well the views of the Minister of Railways upon the fiscal question; we know where he stands; we know how he has voted in the legislature of the province of Saskatchewan, and now I ask my hon. friend the Minister of Labour whether, representing the labouring people of this province as well as the rest of the people, he placed the facts in regard to the motor industry fairly before his colleagues, and whether they voted him down or turned him down. He must know the views of labouring men upon this very question. I am going to place on Hansard an article touching this question which appeared in The Labour Leader of April 9 last, and I commend this to the attention of the Minister of Labour, to my hon. friends from Winnipeg (Mr. Woods-worth and Mr. Heaps), and to the hon.

member	for	Kenora-Rainy	River (Mr. Heenan), because they are all named in the article, which is as follows:
The working men of Canada. never had a bed of roses to repose on, nor do they want one, but at least are entitled to and expect a square deal from the government of Canada.
There is 11,389 workers employed in the Willys-Overland, Limited, West Toronto; Durant Motors of Canada. Leaside; General Motors of Canada, Limited, Qshawa; Ford Motor Car Company of Canada, Limited, Out.; Dodge Bros, of Canada, Limited, Toronto; Studebaker Corporation of Canada, Limited, Walkerville, and several assembly plants of the automotive industry located in various Canadian centres have just reason to worry these days and appeal to Canadians generally to rally to their support to try and prevent the Dominion government from passing legislation to take the duty off motor cars made in the United States, so as to reduce their selling price in the Canadian market.
The 11,389 men employed in Canadian motor car factories during 1925 received $17,595,282.44 iin wages. Again there are some 8,000 additional men employed in tire factories and other plants that make parts and accessories for Canadian motor car plants. We have not the wage bill of these extra 8,000 men.
The Canadian motor car manufacturers pay annually to the government about seven and one-half million dollars duty on material they impart. By abolishing the duty on motor cars, this money would be lost to the Dominion treasury. *
This legislation is being introduced to appease the western Progressives, and they want it so badly that they apparently do not care the injury it will inflict on the men employed in the Canadian automobile manufacturing plants. This is absolutely selfish legislation and there is no justification whatever for it.
Jobs are scarce enough in Canada Ito-day without enacting legislation that will take jobs away from thousands of Canadian industrial workers. Besides the men employed in the above-named concerns, there are thousands of other men working dn factories that make parts for these automobile manufacturers, as well as men in paint and varnish (factories, and the hundreds that are making motor car fires in the tire factories of this Dominion. Were the thousands of motor cars that are now made in Canada to be replaced by those made in the United States, they would certainly come to Canada with tires on them and thus add another army to the unemployed.
The sale of motor cars in Canada has not been retarded by the few dollars extra that Canadians have had to pay in the past, as the streets of our cities are to-day crowded with motor vehicles, and everyone knows that the motor industry has been a God-send to the mechanics of Canada. Canadians, therefore, cannot afford to sit idly by and see the jobs of these men slaughtered by the introduction of legislation to remove the present duty on motor cars of the smaller and medium priced varieties.
Eighty-five per cent of the employees of Canadian motor car industries are married men, with families dependent upon them. Must these men, women and children suffer to provide a reduction in price of motor cars to western farmers and other Canadians who are imbued with such selfishness.
We claim it would be an outrage and we appeal to Canadians in every walk of life to get busy and write protests to the government at Ottawa before this legislation is passed. The government has appointed a Tariff board, so why not let this new board report, on the quesetion before any legislation is introduced? This would at least give the working men

The Budget-Mr. Guthrie
of Oshawa, Toronto, Leaside and Fond an opportunity of presenting their case on 6uch a vital question.
We believe the members of the government should be big enough Canadians to overlook the few dollars extra on each car and consider the jobs and homes of the thousands who are dependent on this industry for their citizenship. No citizen will leave Canada if the price of cars remains where it is to-day, but if the duty is removed thousands will have to leave to obtain employment to look after the wants of themselves and their families.
This is an opportunity for Messieurs J. S. Woods-worth, M.P., A. A. Heaps, M.P., and Peter Heenan, M.P., who claim they are representing labour in the House of Commons, to give their aid to the 20,000 motor car mechanics of Canada in retaining their jobs. Canadian labour men will expect these three members of the House to put up a fight to have the matter at least referred to the new Tariff board, so that the employees of the motor car plants of Canada can present their claims to the board.
This is one of the most serious situations that the industrial workers of Canada have 'had to meet, and the Labour Leader makes an earnest plea to Canadians to forget any selfish ideas they may have and join in a joint protest that no government can afford to overlook. Canadians, be real Canadians and help your fellow Canadians who are employed an automotive industries to retain their jobs.
Now I ask my hon. friend the Minister of Labour whether he laid that article before his colleagues when the present reduction of duty was determined upon; I ask whether he, in his present office, should not protect the rights of the labouring men of eastern Canada, or whether he was simply overborne by his western colleagues in the free trade campaign which they have carried on in this country for the last five, ten or fifteen years.
But what is the province of Ontario going to say or do over the situation? What relief can we get? What relief can we expect to get? The government defeated at the polls, its ranks decimated, nine of its ministers gone, four or five months now gone in which to recruit; yet they have produced for the great province of Ontario only one minister, they have placed him into the Department of Labour, and the first thing labour in this country gets is a black eye such as it never got in Canada before.
Mr. Speaker, it is hard to overstate the importance of the motor industry in the province of Ontario. In the city from which I come, and which I have the honour to represent in this House, we have no automobile factory. We do make trucks or bodies which go into an automobile, but we have no automobile factory. Yet last year I find that no less than $1,280,000 was spent by the Ford "Company in the city of Guelph in procuring the various parts necessary for the automobiles . made in Windsor. This sum went for Guelph labour and Guelph material. Look over the list of cities and towns in the province of Ontario and you will find scores of them
which are to a very large extent dependent upon the very motor industry which this present budget is striving to kill. It is an industry with an investment of $60,000,000 of capital in this province, and at one fell swoop the Minister of Finance announces a reduction of 15 per cent upon automobiles up to $1,200 in value. Sir, I am within the mark,
I believe, when I state that a reduction of 15 per cent represents far more than the profit of these companies which are manufacturing automobiles. They cannot stand this reduction of 15 per cent and still operate at a profit. It may be that in years gone by, in the early days before prices became fixed, before competition became keen, very large profits were accumulated by some of these industries ; but it is cot so to-day. Competition to-day is of the keenest order, and I am prepared to state now, on the information I have received, that this 15 per cent reduction represents more than the average annual profits of any concern engaged in the production of these automobiles to-day in the province of Ontario. This reduction is made at one fell swoop, and it may prove a death blow. Why do it? Why jeopardize the livelihood of 12,000 mechanics in these factories, and 8,000 other mechanics working in allied or kindred industries in different parts of Ontario? Why not listen to the appeal of the labour men of this country? These 20,000 operatives represent possibly a population of from 80,000 to 100,000 people in Gntario who are dependent for their livelihood upon this industry. You are placing their employment in jeopardy by the action which you propose to-day.
Mr. Speaker, why is this done now? Have we forgotten that during the course of the last election, on practically every platform of the Liberal party, representations were made to the electors of this country that if the government were returned to power it would appoint a tariff board or a tariff commission, something in the nature of an advisory commission to advise them upon all questions of the customs tariff and upon all matters of taxation? Have we forgotten that within the last two weeks, perhaps only ten da3rs ago, an announcement was made to this House by the Prime Minister of this country that his tariff board had been appointed? He produced in this House the order in council; he named the chairman and the members of the board, and the secretary.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF HON. J. A. ROBB, MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I am sorry, Mr. Speaker, for the misunderstanding, but I am glad to know that I was not in the wrong, because not only was the order in council laid on the table on the 7th of April by the Prime Minister, but he made this statement regarding it:
The order in council in question sets forth the personnel and powers of the board.
And then he gave the names of the members of tire board. That is what I had in mind when I said that within the last two weeks, or possibly ten days this announcement was made by the Prime Minister. It was made on the 7th of April. Now the board was constituted then; at least, on the 7th of this month the names of the board were published in the papers throughout the length and breadth of this Dominion, and men who had been inclined to wonder what action the government might take in regard to the tariff on motor cars said when they saw that announcement: Well, that settles the matter; it will now be investigated by the board; that is what the board is for. That, Mr. Speaker, was the reasonable expectation of every reasonable minded man and woman in Canada. That is what the public expected. That is what the 20.000 workmen engaged in this industry in Ontario expected. That is what the owners of these factories expected. Why did they not get it? Why go through the nonsensical farce of appointing a board, and then at the very first opportunity stultify yourself and repudiate the board you have, appointed? There is something deeper in this matter which these gentlemen know about. There is something under the surface. No rational body of men, if this government be a rational body of men, would treat the public or would treat the House so, or would mislead

The Budget-Mr. Guthrie
the manufacturers of these motor cars as the government has misled them by the announcement of a tariff board to whom all questions were to be referred for investigation and report in order to lift the tariff out of party politics, and then within a week, a brief week, after the announcement in regard to a most important industry, one of the most important in Canada to-day, flout that board in the face, and announce to the people of Canada radical reductions, serious reductions, that may very seriously hamper and possibly destroy that industry.
I am not altogether a worshipper of the idea of a tariff board. I remember that on a former occasion, I think it was in 1912, I moved the six months hoist in this House in regard to another tariff board. I believe that a tariff board can be constituted in this country on the lines laid down by my right hon. leader in a speech last year, which is to be found in revised Hansard of June 2, last. I believe that something may be accomplished on those lines, but I am inclined to think that the effort of the present government in regard to the tariff board is merely to evade responsibility; it is merely one of a hundred instances of "passing the buck" as they say in the language of the streets. I am afraid it would be an unfortunate day for this country if the government, should ever delegate its power to deal with the customs tariff of Canada to any board, or to any body of men not elected by the people. I am inclined to think that notwithstanding the pre-election announcement, notwithstanding the flourish of trumpets in connection with the appointment of this tariff board, so well advertised on the front pages of all the Liberal dailies throughout Canada, it is the merest kind of a subterfuge, that it means nothing and will mean nothing in the commercial life of Canada; that all the government has done has been to appoint a sort of glorified body of civil servants. If that is all they are, why not let the Civil Service Commission appoint them? In my humble judgment the men named on the commission are not men qualified to deal with the matters which will be referred to them. No man has a higher regard, or a greater admiration, for the Hon. George P. Graham than I, but I would laugh at any man who came to me and said that George Graham was a tariff expert. Why, sir, as far back in his public career as we can recall he has been engaged and exclusively engaged in the operation of railways, in the management of the Railways department of this country; not a moment of his time has been devoted to commerce, or to customs, or to cognate 14011-157
questions.	He knows as much about the
customs tariff of this country as I do about the differential calculus, and I know nothing about it. But he, forsooth, is to be the head of this board to lift the tariff out of politics! Why, his chief qualifications for the position is that he is a politician, a very able politician, and that is the reason he has been selected. I have little confidence in this tariff board. Now, I am going 5 p.m. to quote what another man says in regard to a tariff board. Last night I was reading a book recently published by Thomas R. Marshall, Vice President of the United States for eight years under the Wilson administration. He was a low tariff man, a tariff for revenue man. We know they have a tariff board in the United States, and this is the late Mr. Marshall's estimate of that board put in his own rather racy language. He says, and this is to be found at page 240 of his work, Recollections:
The attempt to take the tariff quesction out of politics is mot niearly so successful as the taking of alcohol out of Iboer. As Jong as the congress oif the United States levies the taxes and determines the sources from which the revenues shall be derived, the tariff will remain in -politics. This is not a discussion of the right or the (wrong of it. This is the frank expression of an opinion that a tariff commission is just a'bout as valuable as a letter written by an inmate of an insane hospital. To pretend to organize a commission that will tell -the difference in the cost of production at home and abroad, is no more possible than it is for a one-legged man to dance a hornpipe. He cannot even tell the comparative cost of production and the reason for it, in factories in our own land, our own state, our own community. It depends on the plant, the management and a thousand other things. We shall never have any valuable information from a tariff commission until they find out how to make men and plants alike, and have them all move by common impulse.
And such will be the experience of this government with its tariff board. What does the government intend to refer to that board? I do not know. Certainly it has not referred to that board the one great outstanding feature of the budget speech of to-day, and the one upon which the interest of the province of Ontario is more focussed than upon any other. The whole tendency, the whole fiscal policy, of the King administration, from the day it took office down to .the present time, has been a negation of the established fiscal policy of this country since the year 1879. I am the more surprised that a man who now occupies the high position of Prime Minister of this Dominion, and who sat in the government of the late Sir Wilfrid Laurier between the years 1907 and 1911, should now take this retrograde, this downward step. But he has done it. I said that since the year 1879 the settled fiscal policy of this Dominion was the prin-

The Budget-Mr. Guthrie

ciple of protection, and I abide by that statement. That principle wa3 maintained almost intact until 1896. I remember well the days prior to 1896 and the campaign of that year. I remember talcing part in it with the Liberals. I remember well the speeches made at that time by Mr. Fielding, by Sir Wilfrid Laurier, and by many less notable Liberals throughout (Canada. I remember our craving for free trade. I remember the various definitions of our policy such as "free trade as they have it in England". I remember well the declaration that "the Liberal party will not be content until protection is destroyed root and branch". But what happened in 1896 when Sir Wilfrid Laurier came into power? Did his government change the principle of protection in the fiscal policy of this country? Not they. Sir Wilfrid Laurier was a protectionist. Hardly a change was made in that policy. What did they do? They revised the tariff. They made alteration in this schedule and that schedule, but the net result when the alterations were completed was an average reduction of less than one per cent. In addition to that they brought in a new feature known as the British preference, at first amounting to 25 per cent in favour of Great Britain, but subsequently increased to 33 per cent. That is when I came on the scene, in 1900. I remember well the situation as it then existed in Canada. We had a protective policy suitable to the conditions which then prevailed. We had the same old protected principle in force which had obtained since 1879. And Canada prospered, Canada did well under it. Now I come to an incident showing what happened in 1903. Under the Fielding tariff of 1900, when I came into the House, woollen goods had enjoyed 33 per cent protection, subject to the British preference cutting it down by one third and making it 22 per cent. No sooner had the preference come into force than mills began to close. Men began to lose their jobs. Mills began to run on short time. I wa3 one of a delegation of a number of Ontario mill owners who came to Ottawa and met Sir Wilfrid Laurier, Mr. Fielding and Mr. Paterson. The delegation laid the case before them. Did they turn it down? No. Sir Wilfrid Laurier said: We shall have this matter investigated at once, and they did. With what result? They found that the Canadian woollen men were open to unfair competition in respect of wages and other conditions in Great Britain; the following session the tariff was amended, and the woollen schedule was put at 30 per cent net on all woollen goods coming into Canada from Great Britain. Why was that

done? Was that done for revenue? No, it was done for protection and it worked admirably.
I remember well when the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) came into the House. The woollen schedule stood then at 30 per cent net; he supported it and I supported it. I remember when the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) entered the government of Sir Wilfrid Laurier. The tariff was 30 per cent net on woollens and there it remained. I remember the revision in 1907.

speechtext:
He was a supporter of
this tariff and so was the Prime Minister. Prior to 1911 the tariff remained on the statute book intact and so it remained1 through the Borden administration. It was the policy of protection. So it remained through the Meighen administration. Then we come to the advent of the King government and the very first year after the King government came into power they began tinkering with the tariff schedules. In the first year 2$ per cent was taken off the duty on woollen goods. The Laurier-Fielding tariff that had served the country so well, that had kept the mills so busy, was tinkered with in the first year and reduced to 274 per cent. In the following year there was another cut of 10 per cent in the British preferential bringing the tariff on woollens ^down from 27i per cent to 24.8 per cent net, and what was the result? AH over Canada woollen mills began to close; men lost their jobs, the exodus started to the United States and woollen men would not invest more money. I say to the Minister of Finance:	Look at your imports of woollens for those years. See them gradually rising in this country until last year, according to the government's trade returns of which I have a copy in my hand, we brought in $20,-

The Budget-Mr. Guthrie
000,000 worth of woollen goods from Great Britain, all of vdiich we could have made in Canadian mills if the Prime Minister had had resolution and courage enough to stand by the tariff which he helped to make in 1907. Yes, they supported it then. Why not support it now? Why change it now? They talk of the golden era which Canada enjoyed under the Laurier-Fielding tariff. If we were prosperous then, that prosperity was due to the principle of protection which they maintained in this tariff. Let the Minister of Finance listen to this. Under the Laurier-Fielding tariff, for which he voted and I voted, for which the Prime Minister, who was a member of the government, voted and for which the Minister of Justice voted, mowers and reapers enjoyed a tariff of 174 per cent. But this government has at last cut the tariff down to 6 per cent and the result is that nearly all mowers and reapers used in Canada are coming in from the United States.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF HON. J. A. ROBB, MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Not at all.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF HON. J. A. ROBB, MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I am willing to stand by my statement. Cultivators in the days of the Laurier-Fielding tariff, when the present Prime Minister was a member of the government of that day and supported the tariff in that government, enjoyed a duty of 174 per cent. This government has cut the duty down now to 74 per cent. No wonder that the trade has been almost abandoned in this country and our farmers are very largely being supplied with goods from the United States. Under the Fielding-Laurier tariff the duty on ploughs was maintained at 174 per cent until that government was put out of office in 1911. Now, under the genial smile of the present Minister of Finance, the duty on ploughs is down to 10 per cent. In those golden days under the Laurier-Fielding tariff the duty on wagons was maintained at 25 per cent. Now, through the tariff tinkering of this administration, that duty is cut down to 12 per cent; wagon factories of Ontario are very largely closed up, and wagons are coming in from the United States. The duty on cottons has received a cut of 24 per cent and 10 per cent on the British preferential tariff from the old Laurier-Fielding tariff. I believe I am within the mark when 'I say that the industrial difficulties of the Dominion of Canada, the handicaps from which we have suffered in the last four years, are due if not entirely, to by far the largest extent, to the tariff manipulation and tariff tinkering of the King government. In every instance in which this government has laid its unholy hands on the Laurier-Fielding tariff it has been to the detriment and disadvantage of the Dominion of Canada.
I cannot altogether absolve in my mind the Conservative administration which took power in 1912. There was a time-and I was one of those who believed it at the time and I think my right hon. leader was for a time tainted with a bit of the same heresy-when some people thought the duty on agricultural implements was too high and the Borden administration, when they took power in this country, undertook to reduce it. Therefore, a small part of the reduction from the Laurier-Fielding tariff took place while Sir Thomas White was Minister of Finance of Canada. I remember on one occasion making a speech in this House in regard to the matter and I remember strongly supporting the idea that duties were too high on agricultural implements. But in that respect I can only say what I did before. Sometimes I am challenged and asked why ten years ago or fifteen years ago I expressed opinions entirely contrary to what I express to-day. In that regard I can only reply in the language of John Morley or better known at his death as Earl Morley when he said: "When I am confronted on the platforms of this country by men who say: 'Why Mr. Morley, ten years ago or fifteen years ago you shared other opinions and expressed them,' I reply: 'My good friend, I cheerfully admit that ten years ago or fifteen years ago I held many opinions which I do not entertain to-day and if anyone can derive any consolation from my discarded opinions, they are entirely welcome to them.' " I repeat, however, that the real damage has been done by the King government which, from the moment it took power, resolutely set its face towards the free-trade goal and allowed its supporters in this House to announce that the death knell of protection had now been sounded. With three ministers in this House from the important province of Saskatchewan, all of the same opinion, three outstanding men ready to ring the death knell of protection and establish free trade, what hope is there for the province of Ontario, with its single little Minister of Labour, no matter how able or how diligent he may be. Under these circumstances, what chance is there for us in the great industrial province of Ontario to meet a situation such as has arisen in this House to-day in regard to one of the greatest of Ontario's industries?
Sir, there is one other omission from the budget statement in regard to which we have heard rumours on the street. We thought that at last this government had awakened to the fact that there was a class in this country known as agriculturists, a class which, in the eastern provinces at least, has now become thoroughly protectionist in its tariff views
The Budget-Mr. Guthrie

and is demanding, through its associations and through its representatives in this House, some action to protect our farmers against unfair competition. There were men, I say, who believed that the government had at last become aware of the situation. In Ontario the great agricultural class is to-day thoroughly protectionist in its views. Look over this House and you will verify that assertion: agricultural riding after agricultural riding has returned to parliament a member pledged to support the principle of protection, e on this side of the House believe also that in the great sister province of Quebec the preponderance of the popular vote is protectionist. We know that at the last general election the question of protection was not made the foremost issue in that province, and we believe that in its heart of hearts the province of Quebec would pronounce to-morrow in favour of the fiscal policy of protection and as opposed to such reductions as are now announced, such tariff tinkering as has taken place, looking ultimately to the goal of free trade, a dream which hon. members in the government will seek some day to realize. We believe that the eastern provinces, represented as they are in this House by a body of members holding a common view, returned those members to the House of Commons chiefly for the reason that they subscribe to the doctrine of protection. Many and many a farmer riding is represented in this House by a straight Conservative protectionist, and we heard rumours as late as this morning that something might be done in the tariff for agriculture.
There was a time when even farmers themselves were wont to say that you could not protect agriculture. The farming community has abandoned that view and to-day it finds itself confronted by a government which, instead of making an attempt to protect the farmers' market in the Dominion, is year by year opening the door wider and wider until the little measure of protection which formerly remained in our customs tariff has now practically disappeared. It is well within the mark to say that the markets of Canada in respect of agricultural products are practically free to Australia and New Zealand and almost freely open to our great competitor the United States. All these markets are closed to our agricultural products. Time was, ten, fifteen or twenty years ago, when the customs tariff on agricultural products such as fruit, vegetables and the like, as between Canada and the United States contained a modest element of protection to Canadian farmers. But conditions have changed; the whole system of production has changed, there has been a

difference in population. To-day our customs tariff as regards agriculture is absolutely negligible so far as the protective incidence is concerned. Look at the hundreds of millions of dollars' worth of agricultural products that are coming into Canada annually from the United States of which a very large percentage could be produced in this country.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF HON. J. A. ROBB, MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: My hon. friend is right. In 1922, for which his party must be credited with the operations of nine months, our importation of raw cotton amounted to 95,000000 pounds and in 1925 to over 100,000,000 pounds.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF HON. J. A. ROBB, MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I was speaking of things which we could produce ourselves. For the benefit of the Minister of Finance and in order to make myseif clear, let me say that I do not include tropical products such as sugar, molasses, fruits, cotton and other commodities, which by reason of our northern climate we cannot produce. But there are hundreds of millions of imports from the United States of agricultural commodities which we do produce in this country, and it is against these things that the farmers of the entire Dominion, certainly those of eastern Canada, want a reasonable tariff barrier for their own protection. Geography is largely against us, and so are climatic conditions; we are under Nature's handicap. Ana that handicap is aggravated by the fact that we have a population of 112,000,000 competing against us. The market to the south of us is closed to the producers of Canada by artificial means.
Why can we not adopt something of the policy of our neighbours in our fiscal arrangements? You must give credit to the people of the United States when it comes to the question of legislation on fiscal matters. They legislate exclusively for their own people, paying no regard to the tariff of Canada or of any other country in the world. If they require an article in the United States for their own purposes they make its importation free, and that is the reason why our pulp-wood, our mineral ores, our asbestos and our electrical power can go in free of duty. They want those things and they allow them to come in without paying a duty. That is their tariff policy, but their tariff policy does not help Canada in the slightest. The moment a hand touches any raw material in the United States, the moment a machine is turned upon the development of that material, then automatically their tariff operates and their market is barred to us. The result is that to-day millions upon millions of dollars' worth of manufactured products are coming into this country from the United

The Budget-Mr. Guthrie
States, .products the raw material of which we furnish them. We buy back the finished article for use in Canada.	Do you not
realize that the people of the United States underetand quite well the situation over here? They are not making any mistake in their estimate of the King government. Here is an official document from Washington-the bulletin of the United States Department of Commerce prepared by government officials and placed in the hands of the president. Under date November 3, 1924, at page 265, the bulletin makes this statement:
Economically and socially Canada may be considered as a northern extension of the United States, our trade with Canada being in many respects moire like domestic trade than our foreign tirade with other countries. The movement of industrial raw material from Canada into the United States and the return flow of a miscellaneous assortment of manufactured goods is not unlike a similar flow between the west and the south and the more industirialiized eastern part of itthe United States.
That is an official document laid before the President of the United States. And how has it come about that such a statement can be possible? It has been made possible by the insane fiscal policy which the King government has pursued during the past four years. Now I am going to read from the Commerce report of the United States of the same date. Oh, I tell you they understand our situation here, they realize the tendencies of the King government and what they are getting out of it. This is what the document says:
Against the set (policy of (the Conservative party of building up a thoroughly protective tariff to favour Canadian industries, has been operating the influence of the Liberal party who stand for a moderate level of import duties and a generous measure of preference to empire products.
Since the return -to power in 1921 of the the Liberal government under Mr. Mackenzie King the administrative efforts have been bent toward a discriminating downward revision of the tariff in which the government appears to have had the support of the Progressive element. The Canadian tariff is subject to revision each spring when the Minister of Finance presents to parliament the budget embodying the general financial programme of the administration for the year ahead. Each of the three budgets presented by the present government have carried changes in the Canadian import duties and almost invariably downward.
United States manufacturers have been the principal suppliers to Canada of most of the classes o-f goods on which the duties into Canada have been reduced during the past three years.
Does the government not appreciate the only result of the course it is pursuing? Does it not see the end of the journey? Why, we are drifting, drifting each year, and unfortunately there is only one direction in which we can drift and that is to the south. Is it too late for us to take a stand upon this matter and re-establish ourselves in this our birthright? I for one protest against any condition pertaining in this country which enables public officials of another country to print articles such as I have just read to this House. I protest against any government which permits conditions to prevail in Canada to which articles of this kind have any application whatever. But it is a sad thing, a lamentable thing, a melancholy thing that we have to admit a large element of truth in these articles which I have read, and which were written by the officials of the United States government. Unfortunately there is too much truth in them. That is the part that hurts, that is the part that stings, and that is the part that, for the last four years, has been doing tremendous injury to the Dominion.
I rejoice, Mr. Speaker, over another matter which I had almost forgotten to mention, and that is in regard to the excellent showing which the Minister of Finance was able to announce in respect to the Canadian National Railway system. It comes as a matter of congratulation to my mind. I am sure it will come doubly so to the mind of my right hon. friend and leader, who is really the father of the Canadian National Railway system. Those of us who have been in this House, say, from 1911 down to the present time realize the sustained, the able, the persistent fight against great odds which was made by my right hon. leader to take possession of the old Canadian Northern and the old Grand Trunk and to consolidate them into one splendid national railway system as we have it to-day. Those of us who were here well remember the wonderful fight that he had to make. Part of the time, I regret to say, I voted against him, part of the time I voted with him, and at the conclusion of the long protracted and difficult fight which he put up for the people of Canada during those long and trying years, I felt honoured by the fact that I was a member of the government which consummated the transaction and brought those two railways, which at that time were such tremendous burdens upon the people of Canada, into one magnificent transcontinental system. I well remember from where the chief opposition came. I remember in this House in the sessions of 1919, 1920 and 1921 how he was criticized, how he was condemned, how on occasion after occasion he would have been outvoted had the Liberal party the numbers at that time with which to outvote him. I remember, too, after they obtained power how gingerly they were in taking over the Canadian Northern system or in announcing a policy in regard to it. Why, Sir, our old friend the late Hon. W. C. Kennedy, when he made his first presentation of
The Budget-Mr. Guthrie

railway affairs in the session of 1922 said: The government has resolved to try out this government railway ownership policy which was instituted by the preceding government. He would not commit himself to it, he would not commit the government to it. They were a lukewarm party in regard to government ownership and in regard to the Canadian National Railway system at that time. But now that the dream of my right hon. leader is about to be realized, now that the roads are Becoming something in the nature of an asset to Canada, now that we can look forward to the next five y^ars and with some confidence predict that the time is coming when instead of writing off annually the interest charges as we do to-day those charges will be paid into the treasury,-now that that day has arrived, if there is any man who should be proud of the situation, if there is any man in this country to wnom we should pay tribute in regard to a satisfactory solution of our railway affairs, that man is my right hon. leader.
I realize, Mr. Speaker, that I have not been able on this occasion to deliver anything like the reply to a budget address that the House would expect or that would have been delivered had the hon. member for West York (Sir Henry Drayton) been in his place. He is a man specially equipped for the performance of such a duty. However, I have brought under review the matters that appeal to me, and I have given the House my views upon the subject generally. I thank the House for the patience accorded to me during my somewhat rambling remarks, which I will now conclude.
Mr. Forke moved the adjournment of the debate.
