speechtext: The House resumed, from Friday, March 26, consideration in committee of the proposed resolution with respect to old age pensions.- Hon. Mr. King-Mr. Duff in the chair.

Mr. Chairman, I am altogether opposed to the scheme of old age pensions as placed before the House in this resolution. I can understand an old age pension scheme which depends upon the incapacity of the recipient to earn a living, but unlike every other old age pension scheme with which I have been able to come in contact during a rather extensive search, this scheme altogether eliminates the element of incapacity. It assumes that at seventy years of age every Canadian who has lived in this country for twenty years is utterly incapacitated to earn a living. I object to that assumption, because actual incapacity should be the fundamental principle embodied in any pension scheme.
If incapacity is to be the criterion as to whether parliament shall vote an old age pension list, I then suggest that the petition laid before the House a few days ago asking for pensions to the blind should receive consideration as a part of this general scheme In Nova Scotia we have an institution with which the name of the late Sir Frederick Fraser will ever be connected, in memory of his life work devoted to the blind. In this institution those incapacitated early in life are educated in order to enable them to earn

Old Age Pensions
their living and support their families to almost the remunerative extent of a great number of people who possess their sight. But those who are incapacitated by blindness after the age of twenty years find it most difficult to undertake the educational work necessary to fit them for remunerative occupation from that time on. If, therefore, incapacity should be the criterion, there is no reason why parliament should not undertake to give attention to those who are incapacitated by reason of blindness at such an age as to prevent them from undertaking the educational work necessary to fit them for remunerative employment. Really I can see no reason why, if incapacity is to be the criterion, this country should not igive a pension to every man and woman who is incapacitated physically or mentally. There are a number of pension schemes in connection with railway employment and employment in our industrial life, under which compensation is given to those who, in the work of railway operation or in the pursuit of that special industry, become physically incapacitated. If this country is to pension those who are incapacitated I see no reason why a farmer, for instance, who comes in contact with a mowing machine and is incapacitated to earn his living; why a fisherman, who by accident or otherwise is incapacitated to earn a living; why any person engaged in any industry that he is faithfully prosecuting for the primary purpose of earning a remunerative livelihood and for the further purpose of developing the general industrial life of the country, becoming incapacitated by disease or accident, should not be pensioned.
Further, I object to any general pension scheme being inaugurated in Canada which does not provide for compulsory contribution by the wage earner to a fund which will bear part of the cost of that scheme. I think it a fair proposition to bring before this House that the government, whether federal or provincial, should contribute to a fund to which compulsory payment would be made by employees as well as by employers in industry for the benefit of those engaged in the general industry of this country. But the proposal embodied in this resolution contemplates nothing of the sort. I have examined into a number of schemes. In Great Britain, for instance, I find that there was an amendment made in 1925 to their system of pensions providing for contributory pensions for certain classes of persons who are entitled to participate in that scheme. The cost of such a scheme, of course, is large, but I find that in a number of other countries compulsory contributions
are necessary. For instance, in Austria there is a compulsory system of contribution. In Belgium, insurance is compulsory for all persons who work for an employer at an annual remuneration not exceeding a certain sum. In Bulgaria, compulsory insurance against old age is established. In Chili there is a system of compulsory insurance against old age. In Denmark the recent provisions are for the pensions being paid by the municipalities, only seven-twelfths of the expenses of operation and management being borne by the state. In France there is a compulsory contribution in respect of pensions, except that in the case of mothers who are earning their own living and that of their children there is a deduction from the contribution. In that country contributions are made by the wage-earners and the employer in equal amounts. The employer makes the contribution, but is permitted by the law to deduct one-half from the wages of the employee. In Germany the Old Age Insurance Act passed in 18S9 was the first enactment providing for a national system of compulsory old age insurance. All wage-earners over sixteen years of age in industry, transportation, commerce, agriculture and domestic service, and salaried employees earning annually less than 2,000 marks, must be insured, and must pay from their weekly or monthly wage a certain proportion of the cost of maintaining the insurance system. Even in Greece, in 1922, there was adopted a system of compulsory insurance of wage-earners. In Italy they have compulsory insurance against old age and invalidity. If permanent incapacity to work is proved, pensions are granted at any age provided 120 fortnightly contributions have been paid by the worker into the scheme. The same in Jugo-Slavia, compulsory; Portugal, compulsory; Spain, compulsory, with certain subsidies granted to the scheme by the state; Sweden, compulsory, and so on.
My objection to this scheme as a scheme is that it is not well matured; it has not been carefully considered; it does not provide pensions for those who are incapacitated except by old age at seventy, and at that age they receive a pension whether incapacitated or not; it does not take into consideration the special claims of the blind, of those who are deaf and dumb, or of those who are mentally or physically incapacitated for earning a remunerative weekly, monthly or annual wage. If parliament, therefore, is willing to undertake a thorough and complete system of subsidizing from the treasury of the state those who are incapacitated mentally or physically for earning their livelihood,-and
Old Age Pensions

that is a large undertaking-it is unfair that we should consider simply this one case.
Furthermore, this scheme contemplates that in its operation there shall be co-operation beween the provincial governments and the federal government. I suggest, Mr. Chairman, that in the recent political history of this country we have proceeded1 altogether too far in the way of co-operation between the federal government and the provincial governments in respect, for instance, to road appropriations, which are within the proper jurisdiction and control of local legislatures. The same refers also to certain building schemes in which there was co-operation, but in respect of which the federal treasury, which provided the money, really had little or no control over the management of the funds and little or no supervision over the actual expenditures made. I do not wish to stress the matter, but I went through for several weeks, as counsel, an investigation in my native province of Nova Scotia which clearly disclosed to me that when provincial governments or provincial legislatures are expending moneys which are not raised on their own credit and responsibility, and in respect to which their sole responsibility is that of expenditure, it leads to wasteful expenditure and very wide latitude indeed in the making of those expenditures.
In the province of Quebec provision is made for those who are incapacitated either by old age or otherwise. There we have recognized under the law the family life, and by law there is imposed upon every member of the family the duty of maintaining other members of the family who are incapacitated by old age or by physical or mental disability. That law has proved, I think, a most splendid law, accepted by the whole people, preserving the family life and the responsibilities of family life, and so far as I can ascertain there is no demand from and no need in the province of Qudbec for a federal subsidy to assist in maintaining what I might almost call the corporate existence of family life.
In my own native province of Nova Scotia, there is no need, I think for old age pensions or for pensions to those who are suffering special disability owing to blindness or being deaf and dumb. That province has undertaken for years past to educate its deaf and dumb and blind. That work has been so extremely well managed and so extremely beneficial that it will compare with similar work in any other civilized state in the world. I do not think there is any demand from that province for contributions of this kind in respect of work which they have undertaken as a province and in which the municipalities

assist. They regard this as a provincial and municipal affair and they are prepared, I believe, unless there has been a change of sentiment in recent years, to continue it in the same vigorous and successful way in which they have carried it on in the past-in fact, ever since I was a child almost, although during the last thirty years many improvements have been effected.
If this pension scheme, therefore, is to be supported by the provincial and municipal authorities, the government should come to us with a plan which has been submitted to the provinces and which meets generally with their approval. It is utterly absurd, it seems to me, to present a scheme, such as this, whereby the federal treasury will be bound, even under the limited measure proposed here, to the expenditure of $12,000,000 of annual appropriations, without having secured first the approval and the co-operation of the various provinces which will be expected to contribute the other twelve or thirteen million dollars. If any one province remains out of the scheme, an unequal and unjust burden is placed upon it, as a part of the country as a whole, for the purpose of maintaining this institution in other provinces. Furthermore, it would be grave injustice to the province of Quebec, a constituency of which I have the honour to represent in this House, and would be destructive of the entire traditions of that province, those splendid traditions which have been preserved for a century. I am sure no request has come from the people of Quebec for this scheme.
On these general grounds, therefore, without occupying the attention of the House further for the moment, I wish to express my objection to the scheme as a whole. It has been conceived without due consideration; it has never enlisted the co-operation and approval of the provinces and municipalities, although the former are bound to contribute one-half the amount involved; and finally it has never contemplated providing assistance for those who are just as much entitled to aid as others who, having attained the age of seventy, are incapacitated by physical or mental disability.

I want to dwell for a moment on tlhe point raised by the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George. We all know that under many circumstances there is much to warrant old age pensions, but if there is anything more than another that warrants such pensions it is the fact that old age disables from earning power. Now aside from the fact that the provinces heretofore have taken care of this situation, this being their responsibility under the constitution, this legislation is not framed on the principle of disability at all. As a matter of fact there is no principle of any kind underlying it. If the Dominion is going to step in and assist the provinces in the care of old persons, the Dominion is under just as great a responsibility to step in and assist the provinces to take care of others who are disabled from earning power from any -cause. Indeed, the responsibility in relation to certain other classes is even greater. The man who when he arrives at old age is unable to earn a living may be blameless if he cannot support himself, but there is a presumption in many cases that his condition is due to his own fault; and very often it is, in fact. But the man who through physical affliction, over which he has had no control, is unable to seize the ordinary op-

Old Age Pensions
portunities of life and thus to provide for his old age has a greater call upon the public than he who has let the opportunities of life go by, finding himself at its close without the means of support. In a word, the cry of disability comes with far more force from the man who is robbed in early or in middle life of the ordinary opportunities that are available to all than from him who has failed to take advantage of such opportunities. But those from whom the call comes most insistently, those who have by far the strongest right of appeal to assistance, are ignored by the government. They are told to shift for themselves while others, less deserving, the government is ready to help because by so doing they can get votes and stay in office. And without a whisper of encouragement from the provinces, unless possibly from one, with everything indeed in the way of discouragement, the government are thrusting themselves in and saying to the provinces, "Here [DOT]is the mechanism; you get in and find your place." Is that going to accelerate the arrival of old age pensions? Let the government call a conference to consider the whole question of disability, and if the provinces are not able to take care of the situation and the government desire to assist, they may join; but do not start by discriminating, especially against the most deserving of all.
Now, those are some features of the criticism I make. The government say: We cannot do it ourselves because we are forbidden by the British North America Act. That act seems to be of some use, even in the absence of the former Minister of Labour, who in his day gave us some fearful and wonderful interpretations of it. But if one reads this letter from the Justice department he will find there is nothing in it about disability. If we want to do it we can-I am not advocating it- but there is nothing in the world in the way of disability. Here is what it says:
Referring to your letter of the 12th, instant, asking to be advised with regard to the authority of parliament to legislate on the subject of old age pensions, I may say this subject does not fall specifically within any of the enumerated subjects given to the Dominion under section 91 of the British North America Act, but does in my judgment fall within the subject of "property and civil rights in the province" committed to the provinces under section 92.
That is to say, the British North America Act does not specifically make this the duty of the Dominion. It does under, section 22, enumerate a list of the responsibilities of the provinces within' which this is included. The opinion continues:
I am of opinion therefore that the subject matter of pensions has been entrusted to the provincial legislatures rather than to parliament. I do not mean to
suggest that parliament has not the power to legislate upon the subject so as to assist the provinces or to establish an independent, voluntary scheme, provided that in either case the legislation does not trench upon the subject matter of property and civil rights in -the province, as for example by obligating any province or person to contribute to the scheme.
That is to say, the Dominion government could not pass an act based on the principle of contribution to the extent of saying that whether a man wanted to or not he had to contribute. We cannot do that. But undoubtedly the Dominion parliament could pass an act, saying in effect:	Here is a scheme
which we leave open to all the people of our country who desire to come in; anyone who comes in must pay so much-that is obligatory-if he does not, why he is simply outside the scheme. The Dominion could do that. In a word, there is no real restraint on the Dominion doing it if it wants to. We cannot compel people to come into such a scheme, but nobody would think of doing that anyway. Consequently it is only a sham, to be argued either on the basis of this opinion or on any other basis, that we cannot, if we desire to, lay down the foundation of an act wholly within our competence and our supervision, the entire moneys to be provided, by the parliament of Canada. All that I want to press upon the committee is, that if we do not do it we ought manfully to say: We do not do it because we do not think it is wise. We should not say: We do not do it because there is some constitutional restraint. There is not.
Now, I rose to point out this. When the ministry advocates, in the first place, that this bill is founded upon the report of the committee, well, it argues something for which not a shadow of a fact can be produced in support of; when it argues, secondly, that this is a fair treatment of disabled people- or put it this way, that this bill is based on any principle of equality, any principle that is not discriminatory, why it has no shadow of foundation for its argument. It is discriminatory. It is selecting, I believe- not in every case undeserving instances, for in very many cases they are deserving-but it is selecting a class of cases among which the undeserving would be far more predominate than any other class of disabled people. In short, it is leaving out those whose appeal is far stronger than the appeal of those it would include. And surely when the government argues that it has to have a complicated system of inter-related provinces in its scheme because of a constitutional restraint, it is arguing what is not true. There is no such constitutional restraint at all. The

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I rise to a
point of order. I think my hon. friend is going beyond the mark when he undertakes to tell this House what the Senate will do. My understanding of the rules is that no reference should be made here to the actions of the upper house. My hon. friend is telling us in advance how the Senate proposes to deal with legislation on old age pensions when it comes before that venerable body. I submit he is out of order in so doing.

The right hon. Prime
Minister is wholly wrong in his description of what I said. I said what I felt in my heart, that this government desired and expected the Senate to do something. I did not say what the Senate would do. I will go further and say this: So far as I am concerned if I had any influence with the Senate I would advise them to pass the legislation, even though it is of an abortive character, so that the uselessness of it may recoil upon the government's head.
Now I come back to the resolution. It says:
That before any agreement so made comes into operation, the Governor in Council shall approve the scheme for the administration of pensions proposed to be adopted by the province.
Thus not only the main principles of any legislation but the scheme of administrating it must be submitted to this government for approval. When I say "this gov-9 p.m. emment" I mean the federal government; it does not matter which government it is. We know perfectly well that the federal government may be Conservative or may be Liberal. The provincial government may be of one or the other complexion. There may be a conflict of opinion politically between the provincial and the federal government. A provincial government of Liberal persuasion may pass certain legislation and submit it to the approval of the Governor in Council of a Conservative gov-

Old Age Pensions

ernment at Ottawa, and all the possibilities of political animosity are there so as to render the working together of the two governments impossible. In any case, this type of legislation should not be made subject to a provision of this kind. Further the resolution says:	"no change" whatsoever-the word
"whatsoever" is not in the resolution, but I am putting it in to emphasize the point- "in such scheme shall be made by the province without the consent of the Governor in Council." That is, a provincial legislature having passed a bill for old age pensions and having got it into operation, cannot modify, change or in any way touch that bill without first coming to the federal government and receiving approval by order in council.

If action is to be a joint matter between two governments-and that is the intention of the bill-the federal government being the parent government introducing the legislation, surely as a matter of common sense, if a provincial government wishes to vary the operations of legislation that this parliament will pass, it must have the concurrence of the parent parliament that originated the bill. My hon. friend will not for a moment argue that that is not a proper course to follow if the bill is to be effective.
I am trying to argue that the bill will not be effective.
Unfortunately.

What I am trying to point out is this. We will assume that they get such a bill into operation. If any one legislature out of nine desires to have some clause different from what another legislature has, it cannot have it without the consent of this government. Furthermore, a provincial legislature, for instance British Columbia-and I understand the Hon. John Oliver has intimated that he is prepared to pass an old age pension law-may propose certain legislation satisfactory to the people of British Columbia and acceptable to that legislature. But that legislation might not suit the provineial legislature of Ontario or of Nova Scotia, and unless this government consented to such legislation passed by any one of the three or all of them, it could not become applicable and they could not take advantage of this bill. By attempting to pass a measure of this kind before a conference of the provinces is held and an agreement on the part of those provinces secured, the government are passing a piece of legislation that will be a joke on the statute books of Canada.

I think the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Neill) said that the provinces had been consulted. I have not under my hand the replies of the provinces, but so far as I can recollect-and I will speak subject to correction-I think the majority of those replies are of a character indicating that the provinces do not wish to join in a scheme with the federal authorities.
No.

That is a fair statement as regards all except one, I understand. I will not argue it down to any fine point, but I know that the replies from the provinces do not indicate any real unanimity of opinion.

While there may have been no unanimity in favour of it, opinions were divided throughout the country. But those replies were made before the decision was given by the Department of Justice that the matter was one for the provinces to deal with, and therefore it is much more now to their advantage to agree than it was at that time.

That answer would be all right except for one thing-the Department of Justice did not make such a statement. The whole atmosphere surrounding these replies indicates what I am getting at, namely, that this government in 1924 and again in 1925 ought to have called a conference of the provinces. How could you expect to get any unanimity of opinion by writing nine letters to nine provineial governments asking their opinion on a given subject? You are going to get as many opinions as letters- you write. But if you get nine people around a table to confer on a given question with the federal authorities declaring that they have taken the lead in the matter, then you would have some hope of getting unanimity.
I wish to draw the attention of the committee to the fact that a genuine effort has not been made by the government in this matter. I do not like to indulge in prophecy, but I predict that one year, two years or three years from now this legislation will be a dead letter on the statute books of Canada if it passes both Houses of parliament this year. It is pretty late in the session and perhaps hopeless to get a conference of the provinces, but I would say to the minister: Get a conference of the provinces as soon as possible; even if this legislation passes, get a conference of the provinces and bring them together with the idea of having some

Old Age Pensions
unanimity of opinion so that the parliament of Canada may pass legislation that may be effective.
In connection with this resolution there are other points that might be studied with profit, but I do not wish to detain the House at great length. Clause 2 reads:
That every agreement so made shall continue in force so long as the provincial statute remains in operation-
That of course sounds all right, but a province might pass the legislation; it might draw from this treasury a certain number of quarterly payments for two years, three yea*, five years, and then drop the scheme. It could fail to vote the necessary supply, or repeal the legislation, or drop it, and so it passes off the books and off the scene. As I pointed out before, the very nature of this legislation leaves a province in the position to step in or step out. Let it be a definite agreement by all the provinces to enact such legislation supplemented and assisted by federal legislation and you may have something effective. But I have a suggestion- and I am replying now to the hon. member, not at present in his seat, who asked me a moment ago what suggestion I would make. I would suggest that the federal government determine themselves if they sincerely want to give old age pensions. If they now say they do-and they are sincere in this although I must say I do not read in the pages before me any evidence of sincerity-let them bring in a definitely and exclusively federal old age pension scheme, and I will support it. In fact if I have nothing else, I will support this just as an evidence of my good faith, but I declare to the House again that in supporting this I feel that I am supporting something that is really trifling with the good faith of the old people of this country.

speechtext: In reply to the suggestion just made, my hon. friend's colleague, the hon. member for West Calgary (Mr. Bennett) told us the other night that if we did what he suggests the chances are it would be declared we had no authority to deal with the matter at all; that it was a provincial matter. speechtext: Just as a step towards reaching, as quickly as possible, the point my hon. friend suggests. What is there to prevent the government from having the provinces come together, and assisting them in discussion by placing before them a measure that has already received the approval of this parliament and asking them if it requires amending in order to be wholly acceptable to them? If it does not, we are that much further ahead. If it does, we can have it amended.

That is a very plausible argument. Why did the minister not take the 1924 resolution a year ago to the provinces? Then he might have come here to-night with something that would be effective. I have about as much hope'-I say this with kindness, but quite frankly to the Prime Minister-of evidence on the part of the government of taking this bill to a provincial conference in order to get the co-operation and support of the provinces as I have knowledge of their taking that resolution of 1924. It is for that reason that I have criticized this measure tonight. I believe it will be abortive, but even at that I wish to support it, not because I approve of its terms, but because I regard the following words in the resolution as the only declaration contained in all this legislation that has any degree of clarity or of sincerity, namely, "A measure respecting old age pensions."

The government
professes its sincerity in the desire to pass this legislation. Perhaps the Acting Minister of Labour can tell me whether the legislation foreshadowed by the resolution now before us will include the Yukon and the Northwest Territory. If it does, does not the word "province" in subsection (d) of section four limit the application of the resolution solely to the provinces?

The Yukon and the northwest will be provided for in the bill.
' Mr. BLACK (Yukon): They are not included in this resolution.
They will be, in the bill.

Little remains to be said in reference to the resolution. We have had a lengthy discussion this afternoon and evening following an equally exhaustive debate
Old Age Pensions

when, the resolution was last before the committee, and I fancy the matter has been fairly well covered from every angle. I have no lengthy remarks to offer but I certainly do think that this is a very notable step in the direction of social legislation, and I want to associate myself with the movement. As has been pointed out to-night, the question has been considered at various times from 1907 to the present day. We realize that a great deal of vacillation has marked the movement. The matter has been discussed by this House on different occasions, and it has been debated in our provincial legislatures. But where a scheme of this kind is passed on from one authority to another and back again we can readily see that no definite action will ensue. Somebody must take a definite step or nothing will be done.
The government in my opinion is to be commended upon having taken the initiative in the matter of old age pensions. I agree with some of the things that have been said touching the resolution, which perhaps is not all that might be desired. Some people will argue, for one thing, that the age limit is too high. However, it is a matter for gratification that at least we are taking a step in the right direction, and it is only a question of time until the various improvements which are being advocated will be incorporated in beneficial legislation. I am glad to see that the legislation is meeting with support, for it will assist a class of people who are most in need of the relief which is promised. This is a young country that offers opportunities to those who are anxious to work, but we must not overlook the fact that even in a young country there is a good deal of tragedy in life. This scheme, if I understand it, is designed to alleviate the hardships of those Who are suffering from physical disability and who consequently cannot support themselves.
Not long ago a warm friend of mine found himself in sad straits as a result of a misfortune which he could not possibly have foreseen. Year after year he had faithfully contributed to an insurance scheme, and when the fraternal society of which he was a member collapsed, at least when its financial stability was discovered to be insecure, it was decided, in order to save what wa3 left of the wreck, that men above a certain age should be completely debarred from sharing in the benefits of its insurance. Many men were left destitute in consequence of this appalling tragedy. Not long ago, in the province of British Columbia, a man who had been rated as very wealthy retired after having placed every dollar he possessed in a financial institution which failed. This was one of the great

crashes that occurred in western Canada. This man was well known throughout the province, and when it was learned that as a result of this failure he had lost every cent he had in the world the sympathy of the people went out to him from all parts of the province. But what about the thousands of people in Canada who are left in exactly the same position through financial failures and who, because of their humble station in life, do not receive the same wide sympathy? These people suffer just as severely, but the average citizen in the country learns very little of their tragic fate. The purpose of the present legislation is to come to the assistance of such people, who are certainly entitled to every consideration that can be shown them by this country in their old age. For that reason I support the resolution.

Some of the remarks that have been made on the resolution before the committee have reminded me of other questions upon which perhaps I may be allowed to offer a few comments. The Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) observed to my hon. friend (Mr. Stevens) that if the Senate should attempt to reject this legislation the Senate would certainly hear about it. It occurred to me that we have been hearing similar threats in reference to the Senate for the last two or three years, but we have never seen those threats put into effect. Throughout the last election campaign the Senate was the subject of considerable discussion, so much so that it came to be an important issue for decision in the country. We were told that the government were out to reform the Senate; that was their promise. But like most of the other promises of this government the undertaking to reform the Senate has gone by the board. A conference was to have been held last year to consider the question of Senate reform, but that conference has never been held. Nor was there held any conference such as was recommended by the committee which dealt with the matter of old age pensions.
I want to refer very briefly to another matter. The hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River (Mr. Heenan) has said that the Conservative party has always taken an attitude of opposition to such proposals as the one now before us. May I remind that hon. gentleman that it was the Conservative party in the province of Ontario who instituted the Workmen's Compensation Board which has proved such a great blessing to the working classes of that province.

What I said was that the Conservative party having advocated these things on the platform, I wanted to see its members vote for such measures in the House.

Fo far as I have been able to see, the Conservative party has done more to fulfil its pledges in matters of this kind than any other party. If I mistake not, it was the Conservative party that brought about mothers' pensions in Ontario.
No.

Well then, I am subject to correction. My hon. friend here mentions that it was framed by the Conservative party, and their successors enacted it. However, the Workmen's Compensation Board Act probably has been the most important legislation for the working men of Ontario that has ever been placed upon the statute books of the province, and it was introduced by the Conservative party.
Now, in regard to the principle of this bill, I, like all the other members who have spoken, believe in looking after the old people of this country. I do not think there is a more pitiable tragedy in the world than a man who in his old age is reduced to poverty. I might point out that in China and Japan no such legislation as this is required, because although they are what we call heathen countries, their people hold their ancestors in such reverence that none of their old folk are allowed to go hungry and unsheltered. Under their traditions of ancestor worship their old people must be looked after by any relation, whether he be son or daughter or some more distant connection.
We have a statutory provision to that effect in the province of Quebec.

I am very pleased to hear my hon. friend bring that out. I had intended to refer to the situation in his province. But I was speaking of the attitude of the so-called heathen countries as opposed to that of many of our nominally Christian countries in this regard. After all, old people are very often in a poverty-stricken condition due to several causes, some entirely beyond their control. Sometimes they are indigent owing to unfortunate investments, as happened to many of the depositors of the Home Bank already referred to in this discussion, or to the operations of some swindler; others, again, have always had to struggle along with very low wages. I have some figures before me given by a Mr. Squire, who points out that in the state of Massachusetts, which is one
of the richest in the union, the average per capita income is only $788. He points out also that one in four citizens in that state over sixty-five years of age requires financial assistance. It is rather a striking fact that such a strongly industrial state as Massachusetts should have so large a portion of its people in penury when they reach sixty-five or seventy years of age. Then another cause is improvidence, and naturally we are reluctant to look after those who have been utterly careless with their money. After all, it is difficult to ask those who have provided for their old age to contribute to the support of those who have made no such provision. At the same time, our Christian spirit should prompt us not to neglect even the improvident in their old age.
I find that in different countries there are different types of pensions. There is what is called the service pension-such as this- which is given to all old people who apply for it and can prove their need, and is granted without any contribution on their part either early or late; then there is the contributory pension; and finally the annuity type, such as we have in this Dominion, which the people themselves buy. I shall come back to this point in a moment. But one of the reasons why I think this legislation is premature is that it is not brought forward really with the intention of providing old age pensions, because it does not comply with the report made last year by the Old Age Pensions committee. That committee sat under Mr. Raymond, and my good friend from Parkdale (Mr. Spence) was another member. After going into the question very throughly it brought in a report, the first and most important recommendation of which was that a conference should be held with the premiers of the different provinces to deal with this question. I repeat, that conference was never held. It should have been held before this legislation was brought in because unless you can get the different provinces to co-operate with the Dominion in this scheme, you are going to bring about the injustice which was pointed out by the hon. member for Labelle (Mr. Bourassa), by my hon. friend from St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Cahan) and by the Premier of Quebec -this injustice, that the province which is not taking part in providing old age pensions for its people is to a certain extent paying the bills of the other provinces that do take advantage of the scheme. It is true that the provincial governments were written to by the Dominion authorities some time, I think, before the committee made its report, but I

I may tell my hon. friend from North Winnipeg (Mr. Heaps) that this is not a refusal.
There would seem to be so much difficulty in the way of providing any scheme that would be suitable to all the nine provinces of Canada as to make it almost impossible, and it will be readily understood that if any number of the provinces were to remain out, it would be almost impossible to adopt any scheme that would not subject those provinces within the arrangement to considerable expense that should rightfully be borne by those outside the scheme. I have not heard anybody who did not approve of the principle.
We are not prepared, however, to accept the recommendations of the committee. The three main objections are: (1) We believe that the federal government should assume a larger share in the financing of an old age pension scheme as it is more a federal obligation than a provincial one; (2) We are not satisfied that a non-contributing scheme is the best one; and (3) There is no guarantee that the federal government would continue for a definite time to carry out the mutual arrangements with respect to financing the scheme.
They have not much faith in this government. Then we come to British Columbia, and my recollection is that British Columbia was the only one which gave any encouragement to the scheme. Under date of February 5, 1925, the Minister of Labour, Mr. Manson, writes:
This matter has been carefully considered by the government and also by the provincial legislature at its last session, and the consensus of opinion is that the matter of old age pensions is one entirely in the sphere of the federal parliament-
I was wrong when I said that they were in
favour of the scheme.
.-and this government does not concur in the suggestion made by the committee that a portion of the cost of such pensions be borne by the provincial crown.

I beg to say that the matter has had very serious consideration on the part of this department and the opinion is confirmed that tho matter of old age pensions is a subject for the consideration of the federal and not the provincial parliament.

speechtext: In reference to the answers from the nine provinces, which the hon. gentleman has just read, I might say that those very replies convinced the government of the futility of ever having an old age pension scheme enacted by correspondence with the provinces. We concluded that the best way would be to enact concrete legislation. We thought that was the only way we could get anywhere.

That seems to me an extraordinary way of doing business with any person-to make your agreement first and then ask the other parties to accept it. Why not make your arrangements with the provinces first? The Minister of the Interior came in with a piece of legislation based exactly on the same principle.

I criticized this legislation on exactly the same grounds as I am criticizing the legislation to-day. The land settlers bill was one designed to help to get the settlers on the land, and the Minister of the Interior said he intended, after the act was passed, to discuss the matter with the different provinces. I am making suggestions as to a pension scheme, and I am not opposed to the principle. I am not making factious objections. I object to this bill because I consider it is merely a gesture, thrown out for the purpose of proving
