that my good friend the Prime Minister wrote what he meant in that book he published some eight or ten years ago, which he read the other evening when he was discussing the matter, and showed by that-and I do not criticize his sincerity-that he believed in old age pensions when he wrote the book. But what struck me then was the fact that he waited until he was in such a position that he could not carry out the scheme without the support of the independent group in this House before he brought in the legislation. It seemed a little inconsistent, if he believed as strongly in the principle as he said he did, that he should wait until this time to bring forward the legislation. I have an idea that this legislation is only a gesture, the same as the wheat board was a gesture, and the Trusts and Combines Act was a gesture, the Petersen contract and freight rates legislation. All these matters were important so far as the Dominion is concerned; they were all brought before the House and put through, but nothing was ever done with them. They were pigeonholed and were of no service to anybody, except perhaps they were the means of giving a little more salary to the civil servants and occasioned more expense by keeping the House sitting a little longer. This is not a scheme for old age pensions. It is a scheme for old age government. It is a scheme to convince this House that this government is out to help get old age pensions, whereas the government knows it cannot he carried into effect unless nine provinces agree; and it cannot be carried out unless it is a practical piece of legislation. If they had the consensus of opinion of the provinces in favour of it, no doubt it would pass' the Senate and pass this House. But they have not the agreement of the provinces, in fact they have the opposition of the provinces, including Quebec.
I repeat that I favour the principle involved, and I believe that, as so-called Christians, we should look after our old people. We should not allow our aged to be down and out and to be dependent upon charity.
What would the hon. member suggest, to -make the bill practicable, or to make old age pensions practicable?
A conference of the provinces. Let that conference be held, as suggested by the committee, to discuss the matter.
Would you wait until all the provinces agreed upon an act before you put it through?

I would wait for one or two of them. When we do not get one out of the nine agreeing, it is a poor outlook. I 
have read the report. We do not get any of them to agree. Why should the government endeavour to put this legislation through when none of the provinces agree?
Was there not a case some years ago where the Dominion government passed an act without the consent of the provinces, and subsequently the provinces consented to come under the provisions of the act?

That is a different principle. There are conditions under which this government has a right to legislate. My good friend from Comox-Alberni quoted a decision of the Department of Justice, and I think correctly, that this is a matter for the provinces and not for the Dominion.
I think my hon. friends opposite are at variance with each other on this question.
Who is?

My hon. friend is not in
agreement with his right hon. leader.

I do not mind that. We have a good independent party, and have the courage to voice our own opinions. We are not under anybody's whip, so far as agreeing with anybody is concerned. We vote according to our convictions over here, but my hon. friends on the other side simply vote to keep themselves in power. That is the difference between that party and this. My hon. friend is not long in the House yet, but he will learn that shortly.
In addition to the points which I have brought out, there is this, which I think is most important of all. This scheme when it comes into effect should be made a contributory scheme. It should be a scheme in which the men themselves, as they go on working in their healthy time of life, will contribute something to look after themselves in their old age. That encourages the principle of personal thrift, and that is something we should encourage so far as we are able. I know what my hon. friend from Comox-Alberni is going to ask me: What about the old people of to-day?

I was not going to ask
anything.
I thought my hon. friend was getting up to ask a question.

If the hon. gentleman would
sit down, I would get up.

Old Age Pensions

My hon. friend is up a
good deal in the House. I think I will stay up and keep him down a little while. The principle of personal thrift is important to people all over the world, not only to our own people. I have noticed that Great Britain after having had an old age pension scheme in force since about 1908, last year brought in an amendment to their act making the scheme contributory.
No.

A compulsory contributory
scheme.

My hon. friend from St.
Lawrence-St. George says it is even stronger than 1 put it. I will get the authority and show my hon. friend that I am correct. Germany has had an old age pension scheme since 1889, and their scheme has always been contributory. Sweden, Italy, Belgium, and many other countries have contributory schemes. Australia, New Zealand, and England up to last year, have non-contributory schemes, where the pension is provided without the pensioner contributing anything. But I submit that the proper system is the contributory system, whereby men are encouraged in their youth to save for their old age by contributing. Contributions might also be made by employers, and as well there should be assistance by the state.
I have offered these constructive suggestions, but the most important to my mind are these two: First, the system should be contributory, and secondly, we should get the provinces to agree before we insist on taking them into this scheme.

I rise to express my
approval of this resolution. I see no reason whatever to doubt the sincerity of the government. I have every reason to believe that if this resolution is put into effect a great many people in our country will benefit thereby. I quite realize that it does not cover the whole field. It does not provide for all those who are incapacitated, but I believe it will provide the necessities of life and some meagre comforts for a class of people who are deserving of more than kind words and good wishes. Some people after reaching the age of seventy find themselves with no provision for their old age. Some have their savings to fall back upon, others are kept by their children; some have insurance, and some are provided for by their employers. The large railway companies, for instance, not only provide compensation for a man who is injured, but pensions for men who have been a certain number of years in
the service. The brotherhoods also provide pensions, on a contributory basis, for men who have reached a certain age, and pensions as well for those who are totally or partially incapacitated before reaching that age. Again, some are fortunate enough to have invested in annuities. I would like to point out that a man can secure an annuity of $100 per annum. at the age of 65 by investing at 42 the sum of $357.81. I have recently been in the west, and I find that a great many people are interested in this legislation. I believe that it will meet with the approval both of those who hope to benefit by it and of others as well.
As to the two kinds of schemes, contributory and non-contributory, I find that Australia, New Zealand, Uruguay, Spain, Denmark and Norway all have non-contributory schemes. Some of the states across the line also have non-contributory schemes. The recent amendment to the British act provides for both contributory and non-contributory schemes. I think that a good number of people will be disappointed because in order to participate in these pensions they must have lived in Canada twenty years. Yet Australia has the same number of years in its scheme, New Zealand has twenty-five years, and Uruguay about fifteen.
Some hon. members referred to the question of cost. I believe it will be much less than $11,000,000. In view of the financial report which we had this afternoon, it seems to me that Canada at the present time is in a good position to initiate legislation of this kind, so that the federal government will have something definite and concrete to present to the provinces when they meet in conference.
Primitive people, Mr. Chairman, are not always kind or grateful to their old people. We in the west know of a case of an Indian woman who cut her own flesh to provide bait to catch fish for herself and her starving children, and yet that same woman died in want neglected by those very children she had helped in that way. It seems to me that as the family advances this filial duty is observed more generally. The state, which is a larger family, should also recognize its duty to look after the old people, and such recognition as this will not only mark a distinct advance in our civilization, but will also reflect credit on those who assist it passing this legislation.

May I be permitted, Mr. Chairman, to read just one sentence to correct a statement made by the hon. member for Oomox-Albemi 7 I have here the memor-
Old Age Pensions

andum issued by the Labour department in which I find that:
In Great Britain the Old Age Pensions Act of 1908 established a non-contributory system of pensions. This act was amended in 1911, 1919, 1924, and again in 1925, the last amendment providing for contributory pensions for certain classes of persons.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: May I ask my hon. friend if he has read the English act of 1925? He will find, if he does, that as respects the very class we hope to serve in this legislation, namely, those who are already in advanced years, the English act provides for the state looking after them without any contribution.

I was just answering the
point of my hon. friend from Comox-Al-berni.

Coming from a large
municipality where we have a number of old people who are in need of assistance of this kind, I support without any hesitation the principle of an old age pension. This is not a new subject at all. It has been before the municipalities of the province for a great number of years. Many countries have adopted an old age pension scheme-England), Belgium, France, Italy, New Zealand, Australia, and many other countries. Stanley Baldwin, the head of a Conservative government in Great Britain, is a believer in social legislation. In the province of Ontario, the late Sir James Whitney was in favour of the principle of an old age pension. It is pretty nearly time that this parliament, which is ready to spend millions and millions of dollars on transcontinental railways that are not needed, and on breakwaters and other material things of that kind, should do something for humanity, but when a question of this kind comes up, the British North America Act is trotted out and made a political football of, just because the country is asked to do something for humanity. We have millions to squander on material things, but not one dollar to relieve the aged, the blind, the poor and the suffering. The time has come when the federal parliament should take up and deal with many of these questions. It should relieve the municipalities of Canada of much of the burden of taxation which they incur in attempting to cope with social problems. The trouble in the past-we saw it in the case of technical education and other questions-has been that politics has been allowed to creep in and issues which should have been treated without partisanship have become political footballs. Timely action will produce the most beneficial results; an ounce of prevention is worth a pound of cure. In the larger

centres they have learned to value and now appreciate highly steps taken to promote the welfare of the citizens and the masses of people generally. I allude especially to the creation of health departments, effective disposal of sewage, the installation of a good water supply, the establishment of hospitals, and measures of this character. The municipalities of this country are already heavily burdened in attempting to care for the aged, the infirm, the poor and the blind. The provinces receive large subsidies from the federal authorities, but often they are too prone to shift the burden they should carry on to the shoulders of the municipality.
Some effective means should be adopted through a system of old age pensions to provide for the aged poor. It should not be regarded at all in the light of a dole. In our large cities probably fifty or sixty per cent of the aged poor people are physically unfitted to work or to earn their own livelihood. The House of Providence, the House of Industry, and other charities are doing a splendid work. I want to pay a tribute to the House of Providence in Toronto, a Catholic institution. It is doing a fine work caring for all classes of people regardless of the denomination to which they belong. When I think of necessitous cases I have in mind the case of an old man named Michael Brophy, a Crimean veteran, who had served the empire for years. In spite of his long and faithful services he received no pension and, at the age of eighty-six, died in front of Eaton's store while engaged in selling bootlaces and lead pencils. It is lamentable that cases of this kind should occur. The officials of the health departments of our large cities know something of the struggles of our poor and aged people to maintain a precarious existence. The cost of food, the high rents, the lack of work, render it almost impossible for these people to live. Even if they were physically fit to work, the employers of labour demand younger people.
This is not a question in connection with which there should be any politics. You cannot keep the life in people on politics. With all the resources at its disposal it surely is not impossible for the federal government to obtain the necessary money to deal with this question adequately and efficiently. And when we are providing for the necessities of the poor we should not omit to care
10 p.m. for the blind. They must be looked after especially in view of the danger which exists by reason of the congestion of traffic in our streets. Even a person in possession of all his faculties finds

Old Age Pensions
our streets dangerous at times, and the peril is even greater in the case of a blind person. Let the federal authority come to the aid of the provinces and the municipalities not only in the matter of old age pensions but in other humanitarian movements the expenditures upon which are in many cases a serious burden to municipalities. Conditions are changing and it is becoming harder all the time to make a living. . The more this country grows, the more we shall find it necessary, whether under the British North America Act or not, to take this up as a question of federal legislation. The fathers of confederation when they drafted the British North America Act could not foresee these things. At the present time these poor people are being taken care of in provincial and municipal institutions to which public spirited people subscribe out of their own pockets, but this work should not have to be done by people with kind hearts putting their hands into their pockets. This is government work, government responsibility and some government should be saddled with the expense of it. It is a movement that should be three-sided. It should be taken up by the Dominion government, the provinces, and in my opinion the larger municipalities should also contribute something to it.
We have heard the same arguments used against this legislation as were used against workmen's compensation, good roads, technical education and mothers' pensions. Dear knows that the scheme of mothers' pensions in Ontario was a God-send to the poorer people of that province-for instance, a widow with five or six small children in a large centre of population struggling to make a living by doing scrubbing and that kind of thing. Apparently millions in cash and land subsidies by the Dominion and by the provinces can be given to railway corporations, and a country that can spend two billions of dollars on a national railway and other projects of that kind can surely do something to help these poor people in these dark days of civilization when it is hard to make a living. The government should come to the help of the larger municipalities especially which are saddled with this burden to the great cost of the municipal taxpayer. I do not care whether there is politics in this bill or not. Politics does not make any difference to me in a proposition like this because it is a question which should be above the realm of politics. I have seen over a period of seventeen years something of the work of a municipal health officer in a council which has been most generous in regard to this matter. Ninety per cent of these people are not fit to work; tihey have been
driven to the wall, and if this parliament is not going to help them the public-spirited people of the country will have to continue helping them as they have been doing.

I am glad' to hear the remarks of the last speaker (Mr. Church) and I congratulate him on the attitude he has taken along with a few other hon. members on that side of the House. I wish to explain the statement made by the hon. member for Fort William and I think earlier in the evening stated by someone else, that the British old age pension system is contributory, and compulsory at that. That is a sort of play upon words; it is both true and false at the same time. The system is this: Britain has had an old age pension plan for some sixteen years. During all that time the age was seventy and the plan was entirely without contribution. Five or six years ago they also introduced a system of contributory insurance against unemployment, or at least against sickness and accident. This was entirely a contributory matter and very limited in its action. You got a pension for only a few weeks' illness and so on. That had nothing whatever to do with the old age pension which began and still begins at seventy and which is entirely free.
As an bon. member mentioned, last year they passed another act dealing with the period between sixty-five and seventy and they made that in some part contributory. It was also mixed up, I think, with some other phase of sickness insurance. But when the person who contributed between the years of sixty-five and seventy reaches seventy, he automatically passes under this free pension system beginning at seventy. Consequently, if we compare that system with the system proposed in this resolution, it is perfectly correct, * logical, accurate and truthful to say that the British system is not contributory inasmuch as when they reach the age at which our scheme proposes to commence, there is no contribution.
I should like to dwell for a moment on the emphasis that was given to those questions that were sent out to the different provinces and to explain that those questions were sent out in the summer and fall of 1924, asking the opinion of the provinces, and the answers that have been read in the House were more or less not in favour of the bill. One or two were; some were doubtful and one or two were flatly against it. I think the reply from British Columbia was more decidedly against it than any of them. It said:
This government does not concur in the suggestion made by the committee that a portion of the cost of such pensions be borne by the provincial crown.
Old Age Pensions

Further on it says:
The consensus of opinion is that the matter of old age pensions is one entirely in the sphere of the federal parliament.
That was the decision of British Columbia in February, 1925, but since then something happened which changed the attitude of British Columbia and, I think, of the other provinces. The Department of Justice gave an authentic ruling, challenged by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Meighen) but supported toy other members of his party, in which they stated definitely, at least to the layman, that this was a matter for the provinces, and although it did not forbid us to contribute, we could not handle it as a compulsory scheme. That ruling was not available when these more or less ambiguous replies were written. It is available now and this is the change of thought and mind of the British Columbia representatives. The hon. member for Fort William quoted the reply of British Columbia last year.
This is their attitude adopted in the session of November last when they passed this resolution unanimously. I will read only the last part, the effective part of it:
That the necessary steps be taken to formulate some plan, in conjunction with the Dominion government, to provide old age pensions; and that the other provinces of the Dominion be requested to take similar action.
That is an entire change of front due to changed conditions. Previously they thought: Here is the Dominion government asking us to pay 50 per cent of what is their business. Now they find the Dominion is offering the provinces to pay fifty per cent of provincial obligation and they hasten to take advantage of the offer. The resolution goes on:
And be it further resolved, that an humble address be presented to His Honour the Lieutenant Governor, praying that he will cause to be conveyed to the Secretary of State for Canada and the provincial secretaries of the various provinces this preamble and resolution.
Observe that. They are not only willing to lend their assistance and to co-operate with the Dominion, but they are anxious that the other provinces should take the same attitude as British Columbia, and I anticipate the other provinces will act as British Columbia has acted once the matter is brought home to them in that light.
It is somewhat remarkable, the attitude with which this bill has been received on the opposite side of the House, the entirely contradictory character of the criticism that has been offered. Some hon. members are entirely for it. Some admit, for reasons they have some difficulty in explaining, they are

equally strong against it. Sonm say they are strongly in favour of it, but it goes too far. Others say they are strongly in favour of it, but it does not go far enough. One man says it is too expensive while another says that the age at which it should be given should be lower. Some say that it is only a gesture. If it is only a gesture, why combat it so seriously? If there is so much contradiction in the criticism, it suggests there is much good in the bill. I regard this legislation as a genuine attempt to deal with the situation. I hope the government will press this measure through the House at an early date so that when it goes to another body it cannot be met there with the excuse that it is too late in the session to consider it. Give them an opportunity to consider it, and if they throw it out, then I hope the time will have come when this government will take the proper action in the premises.

I have taken a great interest in the question of old age pensions during the past few years, having advocated an allowance of this nature in the province of Ontario, and as my constituents expect me to say something on the present proposal I desire to discuss it briefly. Since coming to parliament I have submitted a personal referendum to my constituents, especially in the rural districts, in an effort to find out what their opinion is on the question. I requested an answer to the following memorandum:
The matter of establishing an old age pension in Canada is now before parliament. As your representative, I am anxious to secure the opinion of my electorate upon this important question. Will you kindly express your sentiments by marking the ballot, hereto attached, and return it to me signed by you, or otherwise as you may wish.
During my election I expressed myself on one or two occasions on this subject. I said that I hoped some time or other to have the privilege of sitting in a parliament which would be asked to discuss an old age pension scheme. To my surprise I found the sentiment of my constituency overwhelmingly in favour of the proposal. The replies were greater in number than I had anticipated and they were two to one in favour of doing something in the matter.
As regards the resolution before the House, while I am in accord with its general principle I must say that the provisions in detail are objectionable. I believe that the Dominion should have a universal and uniform old age pension law. I cannot possibly understand how the Department of Justice could give the opinion that while it would be permissible for the Dominion to pay fifty per

Old Age Pensions
cent of the cost it would be illegal and in contravention of the British North America Act for this government to pay the whole amount. This is a legal point, but I must say that it is beyond my comprehension. I see practical objections to contributory legislation on the part of the provinces. If one or two provinces should refrain from participating we should then have this anomaly that such of the aged in those provinces who might still be earning would be taxed to pay their contribution to the allowance given to old age pensioners in other provinces that were under the scheme. That, of course, would be a manifest injustice and in time it would create such a situation as now exists in the Maritime provinces. Provinces would be contributing to a Dominion obligation in respect of which they were enjoying no benefits and the result would be that compensation would be demanded. This feature of the bill is therefore open to objection.
I rise, however, not to enter into a discussion of the details of the legislation so much as to indicate something of what is being done elsewhere in the matter of old age pensions. In November I wrote a letter to Dr. Riddell, the Canadian representative at Geneva, asking whether he would be good enough to give me such information as had been obtained in that quarter on the subject of old age pensions. The following is his reply:
I beg to acknowledge your letter of the twelfth ult., asking for information regarding old age pensions. I enclose a brief memorandum on invalidity and old age pensions, prepared by the International Labour Office at my request. I am also sending you, under separate cover, a number of texts from the Legislative Senes published by the International Labour Office. I trust that this material will be of use to you, and that you will let me know if I can be of further help.
Yours truly,
W. A. Riddell,
Canadian Advisory Officer.
I would ask that the memorandum to which reference is made in that letter be placed on Hansard so that it may convey to others the information which it has supplied me, giving as it does a synopsis of what is being done throughout the world. The memorandum is rather lengthy but the information it contains is valuable. It shows us the sort of pension scheme that appeals to any particular country, together with information in regard to the percentages of those receiving pensions as well as the varieties of pensions paid, and so forth. There is one sentence with reference to Great Britain which I should like to read. In the Old Country pension legislation was first introduced in
1908 when there were 829,000 people in receipt of pensions, this number being seven per cent of the population. The following is the note which I want to emphasize:
So far as the great majority of the septuagenarian population are concerned the non-contributory pensions provided under the Old Age Pensions Acts 1908-1924 (L.S. 1924, Great Britain 4) will in the course of the next thirty years be replaced by pensions for which the beneficiary ha3 contributed.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I thought I heard my hon. friend say that he would like to place a certain memorandum on Hansard.
This is the memorandum.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I do not wish to deprive my hon. friend of any privilege, but I ought to point out to him that the permission to place memoranda on the record is one which is granted occasionally by the unanimous consent of the House usually to members of the government to enable them to have certain official statements incorporated in the report. The privilege is one which, however, should not be taken advantage of generally, and certainly not in committee on a resolution. If the House were once to adopt the practice of placing documents and memoranda on Hansard, Hansard would soon become over-encumbered, as indeed it is already. There is this further consideration: the purpose of discussions in committee is to enable hon. members to follow the proceedings and to weigh the pros and cons of the different points submitted for consideration and discussion.
I would suggest to my hon. friend that he send his memorandum to the Department of Labour and if it contains valuable data it will be of service to the department. I trust my hon. friend will not press his request.

I am not acquainted with the rules but I thought that, as the memorandum is undoubtedly of value, there would be no objection to its being embodied in the report. I am willing, however, to hand it to the Prime Minister to use it as he may see fit.

The right hon. Prime Minister has raised a point in which, I may say, I concur, but I should like to draw your attention, Sir, -and also his to the fact that the practice of handing in memoranda to Hansard has grown in recent years, and many hon. members have erred or violated the rules. So I should not like my hon. friend (Mr. Kaiser) to be singled out as a sort of victim in this case. Let us stop the practice.
Old Age Pensions

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I appreciate
very much the spirit in which my hon. friend has met my request. I think he understood my purpose in raising the point. I do so because Mr. Speaker himself has recently been discussing with me the practice which unconsciously perhaps has been growing up of hon. members reading their speeches, which is something contrary to the rules of parliament itself.
There was a very good one read a few minutes ago right behind the Prime Minister.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
There have
been very many good ones read; at the same time, to read speeches is not according to the rules of the House.
Certainly not.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Unless we
follow as nearly as we can, with a reasonable degree of latitude, what has seemed in the wisdom of previous parliaments to be the right course, we will soon get our Hansard out of all proportions. Again I wish to thank my hon. friend for the wiay in which he has kindly acceded to the request.

The document is so concise that I do not wish to take up the time of the House reading it. As I said before, I am quite willing that the Prime Minister should look over it, and, if he thinks its insertion in Hansard will be of service fto the House, that it should be inserted. I do think that if we have old age pensions they should be Dominion wide in their application, and I hope we shall make some progress in that direction.

Mr. Chairman, I
realize that we already had a very extended debate on the question of old age pensions.
I do not rise to protract unnecessarily that discussion, but were I to remain silent while such an important measure is under discussion I would be remiss in my duty to my constituents, and especially to the industrial population of eastern Nova Scotia, with whom for a number of years I have maintained the most friendly and sympathetic relations.
Let me say, Sir, that I heartily approve and will ever cheerfully support the principle of old age pensions. Nor do I consider this measure in the light of a charitable contribution by the state towards its aged citizens. Justification for such a measure rests not upon grounds of charity, but rather upon the broader and firmer basis of distributive justice.

There exist between every state and its citizens certain mutual obligations, certain grave responsibilities, which neither party to the social contract may wantonly ignore. It is admitted that the state has the right to demand from its citizens allegiance and service; it also has the right to force them to contribute to the upkeep and maintenance of the body politic in the form of taxation, and when some great national peril threatens its very existence the state has the right to conscript its citizens for national defence.
Now, Mr. Chairman, it is a well established maxim of Christian ethics, recognized in every Christian country, that there can be no rights enjoyed either by a state or individual which do not carry with them corresponding responsibilities; and when you admit that the State has the right to exact allegiance and service from its citizens, to tax them and to conscript them in time of war, you must ipso facto admit that the state has a duty to provide for its citizens if the evening of life finds them helpless and in need. I consider therefore that the state is merely discharging an ethical obligation which it owes to its citizens in providing a measure of old age pensions, and I heartily support that measure.
In regard to the constitutional difficulties in the way, there seems to be an idea that this measure should be taken up and passed by the different provinces. It may be presumptuous for me to disagree with the right hon. leader of the government in his views, but I think a conference with the premiers of the provinces should be held first before you enact any specific form of old age pension legislation, we owe it to the provinces as a matter of courtesy, if not on grounds of justice, since they are paying a part of the cost, to consult them as to what specific measure this government is going to enact. However, I do not argue that point, because I am glad to see the principle enacted in some form or other.
But, Mr. Chairman, I wish to suggest in all candour to the government-and this probably' is my principal reason for rising-that in regard to certain classes of labour the age limit of seventy years should be reduced. We must realize that some people who are engaged in the lighter occupations are still sprightly young blades at seventy; but those engaged in certain other industries-I had in mind men working in steel plants and collieries, and women engaged in the garment making industry-find their physical vigour is greatly impaired when they reach the age of sixty. Therefore I would ask the government to take under

Old Age Pensions
serious consideration the advisability of lowering the age limit from seventy to sixty years with respect to those engaged in coal mining and certain other industries.
However, whether the government does or does not act upon my suggestion in that regard,
I shall certainly support this measure, because I realize that it is by such measures we will succeed in lifting up the manhood of the poor in this land. Let me say in conclusion that whenever a measure is introduced calculated to do that, I will cheerfully give it my support, no matter by whom it is introduced or by whom it is opposed.

Mr. Chairman, the reading
of an opinion by the Minister of Justice would lead one to suppose that the Dominion parliament has no place in providing in its entirety for a plan of old age pensions. I do not think that that can be the correct interpretation of the minister's opinion, because I suppose what he would say is that the Dominion parliament has no right to impose any obligation on the provincial authorities. Perhaps he wTould be good enough to say if I am correct in my view.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: That is it exactly.

I would have thought that
would be the result of his consideration of the question. Now, Mr. Chairman, it does occur to me that there is a good deal to be said in favour of the view taken by some members who have already taken part in this debate that you are only going, if not to defeat, at least to disappoint the expectations of prospective pensioners in trying to carry out a pension scheme under such a bill as this. The reading of the communications from the various provincial governments carries to my mind no hope that we will be able to establish a relationship between the Dominion and each of the nine provinces with respect to this measure.
If there is nothing to prohibit this parliament from supplying all the funds necessary to a proper old age scheme, then I think we should take up the matter in that way. Those who are in favour of old age pensions should meet the issue fairly and squarely and say that this parliament shall provide all the funds; then, I think we would be on our way to having something done, and done soon. But if we are, as the Prime Minister suggests, merely to pass the bill with the idea of sending it on to each legislature in the hope that by conference and discussion with each legislature we will be able to have it put into effect in each province represented, we are embarking on a path that leads a long way
into the future. To me this sort of legislation has a very strong appeal. It has a personal appeal that, in spite of the economic situation, one cannot resist. One has only to see some aged and destitute person, to carry his mind to his own people and consider, what would I think if that person were one of my own family? Personally I cannot face a position like that. If the government thinks this is all it can do at the moment,
I cannot oppose the legislation, but I do think very sincerely that if our minds are set upon a proper system of old age pensions we should not stop with this bill, which promises difficulty and discrimination between provinces; we should rather, as I repeat, take hold of the whole thing ourselves, and see that this House inaugurates a scheme that cannot fail. It follows the trend of modern legislation. It is a departure from the old state where security had little place in life; it removes too the dread of the future which must always overhang those who are without certainty as to what will be their fate when strength fails and their working time is past. It is unfortunate but true that only too often people who have suffered and sacrificed themselves in the upbringing of families find, when their turn comes to be taken care of, that they are not getting the comforts they hoped for or the reward they should have from those for whom they struggled and sacrificed so much. There is no legal objection to it. If the government feels it can go the whole way and provide the money for the scheme throughout the Dominion of Canada I shall be very glad Failing that, and in the hope of getting something, in the hope that the Prime Minister may prove to be right when he says that he is sanguine that it may lead to results, I shall support the measure.

It is quite evident that hon. members on both sides of the House are desirous of doing everything they reasonably can to promote and carry into effect a measure which will be of assistance to the aged as provided in this bill. What I want to say to the minister in charge and to the Prime Minister is that in view of the good feeling on both sides in respect of this measure, and in view of the fact that nothing can be accomplished and brought to a definite conclusion save and except when a certain consideration has been given to the views of the various provinces, some conference should be held. miers of British Columbia and Alberta are on their way to Ottawa, I believe. At all events if he had four or five premiers here and they would care to join in the proposal, I am sure there would be no difficulty in having the bill pass this House unanimously, and no doubt a bill could be framed by arrangement between the provinces and the Dominion, that would be workable. But I do say to my hon. friend that if the premiers from the various provinces come along it will be a pleasure to discuss the measure with them.

I do not see the difficulty my right hon. friend suggests. It is not a matter of great concern whether the bill goes through to-night or in a month or six weeks hence. We are going to be here for some time, and we would have every opportunity for the calling of a conference of representatives of the various provinces to deal with the matter in such a way that there would be some finality. In my view the resolution
and the scheme of an old age pension implies that there is something wrong in the wageearning conditions of this young country.
The world over.

The very fact that a country like Canada, supposed to be a country of opportunity, supposed to be a country calling to the effete lands of the east to come over and find their chance in the land of opportunity of the west, has to establish an old age pension scheme shows that there is something radically wrong with our system. But apart altogether from that, I wish to say that I am in absolute sympathy with the principle of the scheme, because we have to face facts as they are.
On the general question I would like to add this for the consideration of the committee. The question has been debated as to whether this is a matter of provincial or federal responsibility. In my view it is a matter of federal responsibility, and I will tell you why. The federal government has complete control ovei the question who is to come into the provinces; the provinces have no control. The provinces are not able to say who shall and who shall not come within their borders, who shall or who shall not settle within their territory. Inasmuch as the federal government has the absolute and sole control of saying who is to come into the province, then it rests upon the federal government, which alone has the power of keeping out undesirable citizens or citizens who are not able to support themselves to provide, as a kind of correlative obligation to this power which they alone have, an old age pension scheme to meet the necessities of the population, the nature of which lies entirely in the hands of the federal government. We in the province of Alberta and we in the city of Edmonton, on the council of which I sat for four years, had year after year to face this question of the relief of those who were not able to work or were not able to get work, and we came to the conclusion which I have just expressed here a minute ago, that inasmuch as we could 14011-159

not put up barriers around the city of Edmonton to say who was to come in or who was not to come in; inasmuch as the provincial government could not put barriers around the boundaries of the province to say who was to come in and who was not to come in, we were not to be held responsible for supporting the people who did come in.
In other words, the authority that has complete control over immigration into this country and the settlement of our provinces and our cities is the authority that ought to deal with this old age problem. That seems to me to be perfectly clear.
On the other matters that have been debated in the course of this discussion, it seems to me that the proper course to be followed should ibe, as already suggested, to postpone any drafting of a bill until there had been a prior conference with the provinces, and for these reasons:	First, because it seems to
stand to reason that if we are going to establish a conjoint scheme in which the provinces and the federal government are to unite, we should consider and consult the wishes of the partners in the scheme. What is suggested here is that we in this House should settle our scheme and then go to the partners and ask them whether they are willing to come in, and if they are hot willing, we should then come back and tinker with the act we have already solemnly passed. Would it not be infinitely better to consult your partners first, to ascertain how far the provinces were prepared to go, and then draft your bill and pass it through this House based on the results of that conference?
There are other grounds that suggest themselves. The provinces have themselves asked that this course be taken. In the replies which were read to the House, and which I am not going to read again, you will find in some of them, in the reply from the province of Nova Scotia, for instance, this:
In view of the importance of the subject matter and the lack of an opportunity fully to consider the same-
That is tantamount to a request by the province of Nova Scotia for time to consider the scheme. Again:
I was instructed to advise you that without a further and better understanding of the subject matter, and without an opportunity to fully discuss it with your committee, no action would be taken on the matter at present.
If that is a sample of the attitude of the provinces, what it amounts to is this:	"We
do not say that we are opposed to any scheme of old age pensions, but we do say that we want an opportunity of considering the question and of consulting with some representative of the federal government so

that we may try to work out a common scheme which will satisfy our province and the other provinces in this Dominion." Is not that reasonable? That is what the provinces ask. But instead of doing what the provinces ask, this parliament is requested by the government to go absolutely in the teeth of the request of the provinces and do something that the provinces never asked us to do. The provinces asked that the matter might be taken up at a conference between the federal government and themselves. The provinces, some of them at least, professed themselves willing to discuss the matter, and the federal government makes answer to that [DOT] request:	We will not discuss it with you;
we will draft and pass our act and submit it to you, and if you do not like it, we will alter it to suit the convenience of one or another or of all of you. Now is that reasonable?
I pass to the suggestions and recommendations of the committee. It was recommended:
That the federal government arrange with the premiers of the different provinces for a conference to held during the coming recess of parliament-
That was in 1925.
-at which an old age pension system shall be given the fullest consideration with a view to securing cooperative action, and that the report of the said conference be laid on the table at the next session of parliament for future consideration and action,
That a copy of this report be forwarded to each premier of the several provinces.
The provinces asked for a conference, your own committee advised a conference; and in the teeth of the request of the provinces, in the teeth of the request of your own committee solemnly passed, and in the teeth of your own promise of a conference, you ask the House to pass a bill without a conference- in direct opposition to your own resolution, to the request of the provinces, and your own promise to pass a bill settling what the terms of this old age pension relief shall be. Now the only answer the Prime Minister makes to that is this: '.Oh, we are in a hurry. We do not want to waste any more time." Why was the timg wasted in 1924? Why was the time wasted in 1925? It seems to be rather another illustration of the old adage:
The devil was sick, the* devil a monk would be;
The devil was well, the devil a monk was he.
You had two years in which to act upon the reports of your own committee, and you do nothing till a quarter way through 1926.
Now, let me address myself to the main question. The only justification alleged by the government for the present course, the only justification suggested for going in the

teeth of the request of the provinces, in the teeth of the government's own promise, in the teeth of the recommendation of their own special committee unanimously passed and adopted by the House, is this: "We are in a hurry, we want this legislation passed quickly." How much force is there in that argument? Absolutely none, because the provincial legislatures are all either up or getting up, and you cannot do anything under this legislation before the end of 1927 or the beginning of 1928. Anyway, you cannot do anything this year. You cannot do anything until the provincial legislatures meet in 1927. The matter will be considered by the provincial legislatures in 1927, and even if you pass this legislation to-day you cannot do a single thing until the end of next year or the beginning of 1928. The whole argument, therefore, that the government is in a hurry, that we should not postpone action until the government has had a chance to consult with the premiers of the different provinces and find out how far the provinces are prepared to go-that argument, that pretext, that excuse, is hardly worth the breath it has taken to voice it.
I understand from what the hon. gentleman says that he is speaking on behalf of his province of Alberta. Would he be good enough to tell the committee what that province is thinking about the matter?

Yes, I will tell my hon. friend. I will quote to the hon. member the answer of the province of Alberta. It is to be found in the report of the special committee of this House in 1925. Under the date of June 2, 1925, the acting premier, Hon. Geo. Hoadley wrote:
Tliis government has reviewed the recommendations of the committee and approve of the general principle of old age pensions.
That is going a certain distance; that is a pledge by Alberta that it approves of the principle. All right. I quote further:
We are not prepared, however, to accept the recommendations of the committee. The three main objections are: (1) We believe that the federal government should assume a larger share in the financing of an old age pension scheme as it is more a federal obligation than a provincial one.
There is one objection which might be dleared up at a round table conference between this government and the premiers of the different provinces.

Is the hon. gentleman in favour of the recommendations as outlined in the report of the committee of this House?

Do you believe Alberta is in favour of or is opposed to old age pensions?

I am reading now, if the hon. member will listen, the reply of the Hon. Geo. Hoadley, acting premier of the province, in which he says:

That must refer to the recommendations of the committee of 1924. Then Mr. Hoadley raises three objections. He says:
We believe that the federal government should assume a larger share in the financing of an old age pension scheme, as it is more a federal obligation than a provincial one.
I have pointed out that the question as to the proportion in which the cost shall be borne as between the federal and the provincial government is a matter of discussion and conference, and of adjustment between the provinces and the federal government when the provinces understand the nature and extent of their obligation. Someone suggested here that the provinces did not understand at the time that the obligation to support the aged was a provincial and not a federal one, and 14011-159i
that when the provinces understood the matter they would be the more willing to fall in line with the federal scheme. Now if tBat be true, or whether it be true or not, it surely stands to reason, taking the Alberta answer as an example-
Was the matter debated in the legislature of Alberta?
The hon. gentleman ought tc know that better than I, because he was a member of that legislature.
I want to see how much you know about it.
If the hon. member will concern himself with what he knows about it, I will concern myself with what I know about it.
The hon. member has just been quoting from a letter of Mr. Hoadley, and I want to know if the legislature debated the question.

I would suggest that if a matter lies within the knowledge of an hon. member he ought not to ask such a question. The hon. member for Wetaskiwin was
11 p.m. a member of the Alberta legislature and whether the matter was discussed there or not he ought to know, unless he was not doing his duty and was out of his place in the house.
Take the other objection:
We are not satisfied that a non-contributory system is the best one.
Surely that is also a matter to be debated around a table in conference. That is one of the fundamental questions of any old age pension scheme. Are you going to make it a contributory system or are you not? If you are going to make it a contributory system, may I say in answer to the hon. member for South Toronto (Mr. Geary), then the federal government cannot frame the scheme because the federal government cannot enforce contributions from the people of Alberta? They have no power or authority over provincial rights in that province. If it is going to be a contributory scheme it will have to be a contributory scheme enforced by the province of Alberta. One of the provinces asks: " Is your scheme to be contributory or not contributory? We are satisfied that the contributory system is the better scheme." Then get together in a conference with representatives of the provincial governments, discuss the question and settle it. Until you have that question settled you do not know whether it should be a federal or a provincial scheme. If you are going to have it as a non-contributory scheme, then it can lie absolutely
Old Age Pensions

within the purview of the authority of the federal parliament. It is only in the event *of its being a contributory scheme that it is *obligatory to bring in the provinces.
Could the Dominion government force legislation on any province in the Dominion?

Surely it stands to reason that the Dominion government cannot force legislation on the provinces. I am not talking of forcing legislation on a province. It is impossible for the Dominion government to enforce a contributory scheme of old age pensions because it has no authority over property rights of individuals in Alberta. You must bring in as supplementary to your scheme some agreement with the province that the province will put the machinery at work for the purpose of carrying out the scheme within its domain.
Could the hon. member tell us how people of seventy years of age who are indigent could contribute to a pension fund at the present time?

The hon. member has utterly mistaken my position. One of the questions at issue raised by Alberta is whether this is or is not to be a contributory scheme. That is a vital question as between the federal government and the provinces. I am not saying which is the better scheme; I am merely pointing out that one province out of nine has an idea that a contributory scheme is better than a non-contributory scheme. So long as that is a moot question, not agreed upon as between any province and the federal government, you cannot settle your legislation. You have, therefore, to have a discussion between the different provinces and the federal government and first of all to settle the question whether this is or is not to be a contributory scheme. Then the question will come up that my hon. friend has raised, and the arguments in favour of a non-contributory scheme. But my hon. friend is premature in arguing it now.. I am merely pointing out the fact that the provinces have not themselves decided which of the two kinds of schemes they want, and until they do, this act is impossible. You must have your conference "first and settle that question.
How could indigent people of the age of seventy now contribute to an old age pension fund?
I am sorry the hon. member has still not got the point. I am not arguing in favour of a contributory scheme. I have not said a word in favour of it.
Does my hon. friend think it would be possible to establish a contributory scheme to meet present needs.

It seems impossible to get it into the heads of hon. members opposite that I am not debating the wisdom or folly of a contributory scheme. I am only saying that some of the provinces have not yet made up their minds which is the proper scheme to adopt and until they have done so you cannot force an act on them; you cannot submit an act which you are sure they will accept. The better way will be to have a conference and thresh out this very question. I have no doubt that if my hon. friends at that conference give their reasons why a contributory scheme is absolutely absurd, their opinions would be welcomed. I am assuming that by " contributions " they mean contributions by the beneficiaries of the scheme and not contributions by the provinces. I am not debating that at all.
The third objection is this:
There is no guarantee that the federal government will carry out the mutual arrangements respecting the financing.
That is already provided for in the resolution. In support of the position which I submitted to the House that the provinces had asked for a conference, may I quote one of the last statements made by the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Neill)? I have not his exact words, but this is the substance of the resolution he cited: He said that in November of last year British Columbia had passed a resolution asking for a conference. In the teeth of that request the House is asked to pass this legislation on the chance that the different provinces will accept it, and if they do not accept it we shall come back here to thresh the whole thing out again and recast the bill. Is the government going to save time in that way? Is it not more likely to get the adhesion of the different portions of this Dominion by consulting them in the first instance before it sets up to them a hard and fast, cast-iron act and asks them to come into it? I know what the attitude of one of the provinces is. They would rather be consulted before the act is drafted than have it put to them after it has been passed by this parliament with the declaration that if it is not suitable it will be recast. The answer would be given at once: Why did you not consult us before you drafted and passed it? It may be said that there was no time to consult them, but the argument of time is gone, because they will say: You "have now to go back and amend the act you have put up to us, and you are no further ahead than if you

Old Age Pensions
had come to us in the first instance. They would have to put through acts themselves, and even if we pass this resolution and the bill that is to be founded on it to-night, we would not get a single result or any action from it until 1928. There is ample time, therefore, in the summer of 1926 to have a conference in order to settle the terms of this bill, and there will be ample time afterwards to pass it.
As I said at the beginning, I am in hearty sympathy with the principle of old age pensions, and like those who have spoken before me, if there is only the one way to get it, namely, by passing the resolution and the bill which the government propose to found on it. I am quite sure the government will have no fault to find with and no criticism to level at the spirit in which members of the party on this side of the House meet their suggestions.

I thoroughly agree with what the hon. member for South Toronto (Mr. Geary) has said in favour of old age pensions, but I am surprised that we should be discussing the inability of this parliament to amend its own constitution. The time has come when we should act rather than talk in this respect. Canada will next year be celebrating the sixtieth anniversary of confederation, and if we do not do something to remedy the present situation we shall continue to suffer under the disability which at present hampers us. The government declares that it is in favour of a revision of our constitution, but so far it has been dilinquent in the matter. Within the last two or three days I have heard the suggestion made in a club in this city that what Canada needs is a Mussolini to take charge of her affairs. Well, if our Mussolini does not come from British Columbia he will come from the province of Quebec.
It has been said that Quebec does not want any change in the constitution, but I do not believe that. In my opinion that province is in favour of such a change, just as the Dominion as a whole is anxious to have it. Session after session this House is held up on various legislative measures because of this very inability of the parliament of Canada to amend its own constitution. I do not want to abolish any rights or privileges that exist under the terms of confederation, but it certainly is anomalous that after sixty years of confederation we are utterly unable to change our own constitution. The United States, the Mother Country, the Dominion of South Africa, Australia, the Irish Free State-all these countries have the power
inherent in themselves to change their own laws at will, but Canada does not enjoy the same right. I have been in this House thirty years now; I have heard this constitutional question discussed time and time again, and it seems to me that the time is ripe for definite action. There is one man in England who is qualifying for the role of Mussolini: I refer to Lloyd George, who some day in the British parliament will do on our behalf what we have not the courage to do for ourselves. If we continue in this state of national impotence this country will fall into disrepute. We profess to be a nation equal with other states, and although other countries and even our sister dominions can amend their own constitutions, Canada remains helpless in this regard. Let us quit talking and get down to action. Let us settle the matter properly once for all. When we do so we shall have taken one long step forward in the interests of the nation.

friend will recall his experience in the ministry he will realize, I am sure, that the government has quite enough to do while the session is in progress w'ithout attempting to hold a conference with the premiers of the provinces. provincial government that may care to enact at once, with respect to old age pensions, legislation in conformity with the requirements of this measure to take advantage of the proposed scheme. My hon. friend from South Winnipeg (Mr. Rogers) has suggested to the Prime Minister a means by which he might possibly get to the point where he could introduce effective legislation of this character. Now, Mr. Chairman, as a layman I should like the Prime Minister or the Minister of

Justice-if in his seat-to state whether he feels that the federal parliament can pass a bill founded on this resolution and then if one or two of the provinces, say Prince Edward Island and British Columbia, accept its provisions, and the remaining seven provinces refuse, the federal parliament can tax those seven provinces. Order.

Some hon. member
says "Order." I have not had very much to say in regard to this, but I purpose to express my views notwithstanding any interruptions of that character. Coming to the resolution itself and what it is presumed to provide, let me say that while I am in favour of a plan whereby every aged person in this country who is not able to take care of himself will be provided for, I am not in favour of any scheme that in principle intends to pauperize any section of the people. As this resolution is framed, the measure to be introduced in pursuance of it involves the pauperization of all our people who will come under its terms. Of all the countries that have tried out old age pension schemes of one character and another, we find that sooner or later fifteen of them have reached the point where they have adopted contributory systems, six have so far gone forward with non-contributory schemes, and one is carrying out a system of forced insurance. provisions of every province and every municipality for the care of old people.

There is another
evidence of the absolute lack of consideration which has been given to this resolution.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Not at all.

I think it was stated
this afternoon that the province of Quebec already takes care of its aged people.
At no cost?

I am not going to
say that the social legislation of that province is not what it should be; it.is for them to determine. What are you going to do with their system? In Ontario some of the very class of people contemplated in this bill are already provided for-in fact they are all provided for in provincial and municipal plans. What are you going to do with those schemes? Are you going to throw them on the scrap heap?
According to information which I very hurriedly secured from the Department of Labour, there are in Canada 220 industrial firms, exclusive of the transportation companies, now providing pension schemes for their employees. Are you going to say to those concerns, "You must scrap your insurance schemes"? No? Then under the provisions of this bill you say to those people, "You continue to provide pensions for all your employees-including the 150,000 railway
employees-and notwithstanding that you are already making that provision, we are going to tax you to provide old age pensions for a similar class of people without requiring them to make any contribution at all."

May I interject that the
employees of the railroads, particularly the brotherhoods that have old age pension schemes of their own and will not be entitled to any benefit under this measure, have gone on record approving of this scheme?

Mr. Chairman, my
hon. friend perhaps speaks for the brotherhoods a little out of his turn. The brotherhoods have considered the question of old age pensions, and they have endorsed the general principle of means being found by which old age pensions will be provided where necessary. But has this scheme been submitted to the brotherhood?
.Mr. STEWART (Edmonton): You are not asking that anyone capable of looking after himself be provided for?
No.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Do you
argue that all the provisions made by the various organizations will be scrapped because provision is being made for old age pensions for people unable to take care of themselves?

Before you undertake
to pass legislation which you will automatically force on the country, you must take these things into consideration. Manifestly this government has not done so. Now, as these various industrial concerns are already paying the costs in connection with insurance schemes and providing funds for vast numbers of employees. I contend that it is wholly unfair to expect them to contribute to old age pensions, for others. Moreover, I question whether you have the jurisdiction.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Does the
hon. member deny that these concerns are now contributing to the upkeep of the indigent?

Yes; that is, they are
nob contributing generally. And are you going to make them contribute to such pensions in addition to the provision they already make? There is no doubt that they will as a result of this legislation; for who will pay the $23,000,000?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Does the
hon. member argue that they are not paying now?
Old Age Pensions
Most assuredly, because they are not being taxed for the purpose.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Then you
say there are no people in Canada who are not able to support themselves?

I speak, of course, of
the province an which I live. When one of the municipalities taxes itself to take care of the indigent, does this not suggest that there are people in that community who are unable to support themselves? In any equitable scheme of old age pensions you work out you must take all these things into consideration, and if it is going to be equitable and successful it must have a contributory basis. The question has been asked, how are you going to take care of people who are now seventy years of age? Does anyone argue that it is impossible to frame an act that will take care of people seventy years of age, and at the same time provide that those under seventy years of age who are in a position to do so shall make contributions to the fund? How is it they have had such a system in Great Britain since 1908?

Would the hon. member
favour the adoption in Canada of the scheme in operation in Great Britain?

I am in favour of a
scheme of old age pensions properly worked out, made contributory on the part of those below a certain age, by which those over that age will be taken care of. I would like to see such a measure introduced in this House with some reasonable assurance that it is going to become law. The hon. member for South Toronto put the case in a nutshell when he suggested that the bill should be withdrawn and the government should introduce a federal measure of old age pensions and take the responsibility of passing it. It is the only way in which it can be done, because you cannot force legislation on the provinces without giving them some say as to the manner in which it shall be framed. This legislation has been introduced for the purpose of side-tracking the whole question. If we live a hundred years we will never see anything practical as the result of it. You cannot force it on the provinces. This federal parliament can introduce legislation providing for old age pensions and put it into effect if they are prepared to pay the whole bill, and that is all they have to do. In 1919 hon. gentlemen opposite pledged themselves to a system of old age pensions and a lot of other things which they have long since
[Mr. Nicholson.!	.
forgotten. They would have forgotten about this matter also had it not been for the two hon. members from Winnipeg, to whom the Prime Minister was forced to yield. But the government forgot all about it in the Speech from the Throne.

Does the hon. gentleman
know, or has he forgotten, that this is not a party question; and that this House in 1923 passed a resolution in favour of old age pensions?
I am not endeavouring to make a party question of if, but if the government will withdraw this wholly innocuous resolution and introduce a workable scheme for old age pensions, I will support it.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: And let the hon. member for East Algoma draft the bill.

You need not get so
jocular over it. Ever since the beginning of the session legislation has been thrown at us without being considered. When members of the government meet around the council table they say to themselves, "What kind of legislation can we draft that will hoodwink the people and hoodwink members of the House of Commons into supporting it?" So far as we can see. this legislation is of that class. The hon. minister who interrupted me a few minutes ago had to withdraw his bill the other day because proper consideration had not been given to it.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I will tell
my hon. friend that legislation in regard to soldiers has always been a subject on which we have tried to get unanimous agreement in the House.

So far this session
government bills have been brought into the House in a half-baked condition, making it impossible for the government-

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
My hon.
friend will not support any government bill unless it suits him personally. It may come to the point where we will have to divide on questions of this kind.

I hope the minister
does not think he has me scared on that account. If he thinks I am afraid to go on record as voting against any government measure, he is badly mistaken.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I will say
to my hon. friend that he need not imagine that he can scare the government.

Hudson's Bay Exploratory Syndicate

I have no intention of scaring the government; I wish simply to express my opinion. When the government brings in legislation which is wholly innocuous and meaningless, designed entirely to sidetrack the whole question, I am going to oppose it.

Is it not a strange position
to take to say the bill was brought in at the instigation of the labour men and yet brought in to fool them?

No, it is not strange
at all. The whole record of the government since they came into office has been to bring in legislation to fool those members supporting the government.

Does the hon. member
think the labour men are so easily fooled?

In the first place, I
do not know that there are any labour men sitting over there, and when the opportunity comes we may have occasion to discuss that question. But whether they are fooled or not fooled, this bill is designed to fool them and designed to fool every other working man who is depending on it.
Resolution reported, read the second time and concurred in. Mr. King (Kootenay) thereupon moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 21, respecting old age pensions.
Motion agreed to and bill read the first time.
On motion of Mr. Mackenzie King the House adjourned at 11.45 p.m.
Friday, April 16, 1926.
